## ECRD 2026: Advancing rare disease policies in a changing and competitive Europe

January 2026

---

**The 13th European Conference on Rare Diseases and Orphan Products (ECRD 2026) will take place in Prague and online on 3 and 4 June under the theme*****“Rare Diseases in a Changing & Competitive Europe: Shaping policies to address the unmet needs of people living with rare diseases”*****. The conference will bring together a broad range of stakeholders to advance concrete policy solutions that improve the lives of people living with a rare disease and their families.**

---

ECRD 2026 will take place at a pivotal moment for the rare disease ecosystem. The conference is set to deliver concrete policy solutions to long-standing challenges through the presentation of a European Blueprint for Rare Diseases. The Blueprint will encompass proposals for an EU Action Plan as well as Europe’s broader contribution to the implementation of the WHO Global Action Plan on Rare Diseases. Participants will help shape the future of rare disease policy in Europe and beyond.

[Register to attend ECRD 2026!](https://www.rare-diseases.eu/register/)

With the conference now less than six months away, we take a closer look at the six thematic tracks that will frame the key discussions at ECRD 2026 and help shape the future of rare disease policy in Europe.

---

While the development of advanced therapies, such as gene and cell therapies, is accelerating, progress remains constrained by small patient populations and fragmented infrastructures. The development of paediatric and orphan medical devices faces similarly complex barriers, including high costs, lengthy conformity assessments, and the risk of market withdrawal despite urgent patient need.

The track on Therapies and Medical Devices, Development and Access will explore this transformative moment in which innovation converges with regulatory reform and collaborative action. We will draw on lessons from ongoing EU-funded initiatives, including RealiseD, Joint4ATMPs, DeCODe, ORPHADEV4KIDS, and i4KIDS-4RARE, as well as key EU policy developments – including reforms to the EU general pharmaceutical legislation, potential revisions to the EU Medical Devices Regulation, the European Life Sciences Strategy, and the EU Biotech Act I. Sessions will examine how more harmonised, patient-centred pathways can support the development of therapies and essential medical devices, and ensure safe, equitable, and timely access across Europe.

---

Many patients endure prolonged diagnostic odysseys, often lasting five to seven years, with misdiagnoses and fragmented care adding to the burden. Despite advances in genomics, multi-omics, and digital tools, access to timely testing, newborn screening, carrier screening, and genetic counselling remains uneven, leaving significant gaps in equity and early intervention.

This track will highlight how new technologies, integrated data systems, and coordinated European strategies can transform early detection and preventive care, while addressing ethical and equity considerations. The objective is to foster actionable solutions that accelerate diagnosis, expand prevention, and support informed, patient-centered decision-making across healthcare systems in Europe.

---

This track will focus on understanding and improving access to evidence-based holistic care for people living with rare diseases – care that integrates clinical, psychological, and social dimensions. Evidence from the Rare Barometer survey shows that while many people do not expect to be cured by 2030, they do expect access to integrated health and social care, psychosocial support, and social inclusion. Research highlights persistent priorities, including better coordination between healthcare professionals, social recognition, and the meaningful involvement of patient organisations in research.

Sessions will explore what evidence exists, where gaps remain, and how insights from social sciences and humanities research, patient surveys, registries, and databases can be better integrated into public policies. Participants will reflect on progress over the past decade and identify strategies to further advance access to holistic care across Europe.

---

This track will explore the multifaceted challenges and opportunities in ensuring timely and equitable access to specialised healthcare services for people living with rare and complex conditions at national and cross-national levels. Insufficient care coordination and persistent socioeconomic and geographic inequities continue to fragment access and make healthcare systems difficult to navigate.

Drawing on the [Rare 2030](https://www.rare2030.eu/) recommendations and existing evidence, sessions will examine innovative health system approaches to optimise access to specialised healthcare services, identify knowledge and data gaps, and provide actionable evidence to support policy decision-making. Speakers will discuss institutional arrangements across countries, as well as the information and metrics policymakers need to assess system performance, improve quality, and design reforms that strengthen access to specialised care.

---

This track will focus on how mental health challenges associated with rare conditions are often misunderstood, under-researched, and excluded from integrated care models. For many rare diseases, mental health is not only a co-morbidity but a core feature, shaped by biological, psychological, and social factors. Families frequently face a lack of support when young people with intellectual disabilities transition out of paediatric care, while adults often lack access to structured neuropsychological assessment and follow-up. Caregivers experience significant stress, isolation, and economic strain, often with limited guidance or systemic support.

The track will highlight persistent clinical, research, and social gaps and explore how mental health needs in rare diseases differ from those of the general population. The track will advance multidisciplinary and cross-country collaboration, helping elevate mental health as a European policy priority and build momentum towards more integrated approaches across care, research, and social systems.

---

This track will focus on preparing for the inclusion of orphan medicinal products in the EU Health Technology Assessment Framework, building on lessons learned from oncology products and advanced therapy medicinal products. With the Regulation fully applied to oncology and ATMPs since January 2025, and ahead of its extension to orphan products in January 2028, stakeholders must now reflect on readiness, remaining challenges, and future impact. This includes people living with rare diseases, clinical experts, and the HTA Coordination Group.

Sessions will examine how joint European clinical assessments are used in national contexts, how to address rare disease-specific challenges such as small patient populations, limited expertise, and potential conflicts of interest, and how people living with rare diseases can meaningfully contribute to joint work. Discussions will also explore how clinical evidence can be generated and assessed to support faster and more equitable access to treatments, and whether assessment processes should differ for rare and ultra-rare diseases compared with more common conditions.

---

## Join us in Prague!

ECRD 2026 will be a key moment for the rare disease ecosystem – turning collective ambition into tangible results for people living with rare diseases. By uniting stakeholders around a shared European Blueprint for Rare Diseases, the conference will help translate advocacy into a practical, action-oriented roadmap that consolidates existing initiatives, addresses gaps, and accelerates progress across Europe.

The conference will also offer a unique platform to showcase innovation, research, and best practices from across the rare disease ecosystem. [Poster abstract submissions](https://www.rare-diseases.eu/posters/) are open until **6 March 2026**, and patient organisations, researchers, healthcare professionals, and other stakeholders are encouraged to share their work and help shape the conversation.

Registration is now open, with **early-bird prices available until 26 February 2026**. Be part of this momentum – join us in Prague or online and [register now](https://www.rare-diseases.eu/register/).

bedrock_calls.system_prompt:
You are an HTA and Market Access strategist extracting structured evidence from one source document for a JCA (Joint Clinical Assessment) comparator and outcome scoping request.

You will be told the REQUESTED INTERVENTION and the REQUESTED POPULATION. Extract every distinct claim the document makes that is relevant to comparator or outcome scoping.

CRITICAL - DO NOT HALLUCINATE:
- Use ONLY information explicitly stated in the provided text. Never use outside medical knowledge to fill a gap, infer a typical dose, assume a standard comparator, or complete a partial fact with what is usually true.
- If a field is not explicitly stated, its value MUST be an empty string. Never invent a value to avoid leaving something blank.
- Do not paraphrase in a way that adds specificity the text did not have.

FIELD DEFINITIONS - read these; they are not self-evident:

subject_drug: the drug this specific claim is ABOUT - the treatment being assessed, studied or recommended in the passage you are extracting from. A document about a disease often discusses several drugs. If the passage is about a DIFFERENT drug than the requested intervention, say so here. Never write the requested intervention's name unless the passage is genuinely about it.

comparator.as_stated: the treatment this claim names as a comparison, alternative or standard of care - exactly as the source words it, including a regimen's full component list. A drug name, a named regimen, or a legitimate generic category the source states as the most specific thing available ("best supportive care", "physician's choice of chemotherapy"). NOT a sentence, NOT a trial name, NOT a statistical annotation.

comparator.role - choose exactly one:
  "active_comparator"  - studied, recommended or required AS the comparison for the subject drug in the population this passage describes
  "prior_therapy"      - treatment the patient RECEIVED BEFORE reaching this population (e.g. an induction regimen preceding a maintenance-phase question). This is treatment history, NOT a comparator
  "background_therapy" - given to all arms as a backbone, not the thing being compared
  "intervention_arm"   - this IS the subject drug's own arm, not a comparator
  "unclear"            - the passage does not let you tell
Getting this wrong is the single most common error: an induction-phase backbone named near the right population is prior therapy, not a comparator.

comparator.components: for a combination regimen, the complete list of substances AS ONE SOURCE STATES THEM. Never pool components from two different regimens that share an ingredient.

comparator.comparator_scenario - from the source's own language, choose one:
  "unique" (names one comparator) | "each_required" (several, required together) |
  "at_least_one" (several, at least one acceptable) | "individualised" (a bundle of options chosen by patient characteristics)

comparator.retain_all_status: "confirmed_droppable" or "confirmed_must_retain" ONLY when the source itself states a droppability preference. Otherwise "unconfirmed" - which will be the case for the great majority of sources, because this is a procedural preference, not a clinical fact. Never infer it.

DO NOT populate any drug class or mechanism for the comparator. That is resolved downstream from the comparator's own substance identity. If you write a class here it will be the SUBJECT drug's class, which is the exact error this instruction prevents.

population_context.*: the disease/population context THE SOURCE ITSELF states for this claim, in the source's own words - distinct from the requested population, which may be broader or narrower. Fill line_of_therapy, prior_therapy, stage, biomarker and treatment_setting_intent with what THIS passage says, never with the requested population's own label. If the passage states an interval since prior therapy or since relapse, put it in "other".

recommendation_strength (clinical guidelines only): "preferred" | "conditional_alternative" | "not_recommended" | "not_stated", as the guideline itself grades it. Never present a conditional or alternative recommendation as preferred.

outcome.measure: the outcome or endpoint named.
outcome.result: the reported figure, if any, exactly as stated.
outcome.unit: the unit of measurement EXACTLY as the source reports it (e.g. "months, median", "% of patients", "HR (95% CI)") - never invented, never assumed from general knowledge of what a typical unit would be.
outcome.instrument: the named instrument, where the source names one (e.g. a specific questionnaire). Empty otherwise.
outcome.is_requirement: true when the source states this outcome as one an assessment REQUIRES or EXPECTS in scope (an HTA methods document, an assessment scope table, a guideline's stated outcome set). false when the source is merely REPORTING a result for it. These are different things and the distinction matters more than the value.
outcome.requirement_type: "relative_effect_required" | "descriptive_only" | "" - only when the source states it.

evidence_quote: a VERBATIM span copied from the text that contains this claim. It must appear character-for-character in the text. If you cannot copy such a span, omit the whole record rather than paraphrasing.
evidence_locator: where in the document it sits (section heading, table number, page), if the text makes that visible.

member_state: the country whose body/guideline this claim belongs to, when the document is a national source. "EU-wide" for an EU-level record. Empty if unclear.

MULTIPLE POPULATIONS IN ONE DOCUMENT: a document can describe several populations for the same drug. Output SEPARATE records, one per population the text actually describes. Each comparator stays attached to the population it was ACTUALLY reported against - never pulled into the requested population's record just because the same document also discusses that population elsewhere.

Return ONLY a JSON array, no preamble, no markdown fences. Empty array if the document contains nothing relevant:
[
  {"finding_type": "comparator",
   "subject_drug": "...",
   "member_state": "",
   "comparator": {"as_stated": "", "role": "active_comparator", "is_combination": false,
                  "components": [], "comparator_scenario": "", "retain_all_status": "unconfirmed"},
   "population_context": {"disease": "", "subtype_histology": "", "stage": "", "biomarker": "",
                          "line_of_therapy": "", "prior_therapy": "",
                          "treatment_setting_intent": "", "age_band": "", "other": "",

Nature Reviews Drug Discovery nature reviews drug discovery https://doi.org/10.1038/s41573-024-01059-3 Review article Check for updates The state-of-the-art of N-of-1 therapies and the IRDiRC N-of-1 development roadmap Anneliene H. Jonker 1, Elena-Alexandra Tataru 2,3, Holm Graessner4, David Dimmock 5, Adam Jaffe6, Gareth Baynam 7,8,9, James Davies 10,11,12, Shruti Mitkus13, Oxana Iliach14,15, Rich Horgan16, Erika F. Augustine17, Alison Bateman-House18, Anna Maria Gerdina Pasmooij19,20, Tim Yu 21, Matthis Synofzik 22,23, Julie Douville24, Larissa Lapteva25, Philip John Brooks26, Daniel O’Connor27, Annemieke Aartsma-Rus28 & on behalf of The N-of-1 Task Force of the International Rare Diseases Research Consortium (IRDiRC)* Abstract In recent years, a small number of people with rare diseases caused by unique genetic variants have been treated with therapies developed specifically for them. This pioneering field of genetic N-of-1 therapies is evolving rapidly, giving hope for the individualized treatment of people living with very rare diseases. In this Review, we outline the concept of N-of-1 individualized therapies, focusing on genetic therapies, and illustrate advances and challenges in the field using cases for which therapies have been successfully developed. We discuss why the traditional drug development and reimbursement pathway is not fit for purpose in this field, and outline the pragmatic, regulatory and ethical challenges this poses for future access to N-of-1 therapies. Finally, we provide a roadmap for N-of-1 individualized therapy development.
Sections Introduction Definition of N-of-1 therapy State-of-the-art of genetic N-of-1 therapies Roadmap for N-of-1 treatment development Outlook A full list of affiliations appears at the end of the paper. *A list of authors and their affiliations appears at the end of the paper. e-mail: A.M.Aartsma-Rus@lumc.nl Nature Reviews Drug Discovery Review article therapy addressing a unique mutation. However, although these muta-tions may be unique at the time of diagnosis and start of individualized therapy development, sometimes a second or third patient with the same mutation will be found. As such, an individualized therapy is expected to address no more than five people with the same mutation. Note that this number is arbitrary and this poses an ethical challenge, as do many aspects related to individualized therapy development19.
An N-of-1 therapy — in the context of genetic therapies — is pre-cisely targeted, typically to an individual’s pathogenic genetic variant or to a polymorphism linked to the pathogenic variant, and typically is designed to address the root genetic cause of the disease by restoring protein function or reducing expression of a dysfunctional protein. Notably, similar to the therapy itself, other components of the develop-ment process probably need to be individualized, such as the selection of outcome measures used to evaluate the efficacy of the therapy, or the approach used to assess the risk and benefit as perceived by people receiving a therapy20.
Many of the challenges encountered in N-of-1 therapy develop-ment overlap with those for rare disease drug development in general — for example, the need to understand the basic molecular mechanism of the disease, limited commercial interest in small populations and the need to rigorously establish clinical benefit and assess potential safety risks. Here, we focus on the opportunities and challenges of N-of-1 therapy development, as the most extreme case21,22 (Fig. 1). However, as the terms personalized medicine and precision medicine are gener-ally applied to groups or subsets of people, we propose to use N-of-1 therapy or individualized therapy to avoid confusion.
N-of-1 therapies, as they are discussed here, should not be con-fused with classical N-of-1 trials, where one or more drugs targeting a disease symptom and a placebo are compared in a single individual in a crossover design. Whereas both are done in hopes of benefitting the patient, the N-of-1 crossover trials are done specifically for research, with the primary goal being the generation of generalizable informa-tion, whereas individualized treatment development is being done specifically for treatment (albeit of an experimental nature), with the primary goal being the well-being of the patient.
State-of-the-art of genetic N-of-1 therapies Several therapeutic modalities, including antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) therapy23,24, gene25 and cell26 therapy, cancer vaccines27 and small-molecule drugs, have been used so far as the basis for develop-ing N-of-1 therapies (Fig. 2). Recombinant proteins28 might also provide options for N-of-1 therapies, and more opportunities are emerging based on rapid advances with technologies such as CRISPR–Cas9 genome editing29. Here, we highlight examples of N-of-1 therapy for several modalities based on cases that have been described in the litera-ture or reported in International Rare Diseases Research Consortium (IRDiRC) Task Force meetings.
Antisense oligonucleotide therapies Currently, ASOs are often considered to be the most mature of the modalities for developing N-of-1 therapies, supported by the strong potential this RNA-targeted platform has for rapid rational design of drug candidates. ASOs can be designed to block production of patho-genic proteins via degradation of the target mRNA, and in some cases it may be possible to design ASOs to restore protein function that has been compromised by mutations that affect RNA splicing (Fig. 2).
Milasen, the first individualized ASO therapy, is an example of an ASO that modulates RNA splicing. It was developed via a clinician-led Introduction Rare diseases can be defined as conditions with a prevalence of fewer than 1 in 2,000 people in any World Health Organization (WHO)-defined region of the world1. However, with approximately 10,000 recognized rare diseases, there are an estimated 250–450 million people living with rare or ultra-rare diseases worldwide2–4. Given this large number of people, it is striking that fewer than 5% of rare diseases have spe-cific pharmacological therapies, and many treatments only address some aspects of the symptoms5. This is due to the challenges related to small population research such as the relative rarity of each disease, heterogeneous presentation, lack of disease knowledge, including lack of natural history data, low commercial interest and regulatory challenges6,7. Furthermore, most rare diseases are much less prevalent than the threshold for rarity, with 85% of rare diseases having a preva-lence of <1 in 1,000,000 and diseases sometimes only being known to affect a single person8.
Over the last few decades, research on therapeutics for rare dis-eases has seen remarkable progress, with the development of specific funding opportunities, dedicated regulatory incentives, improve-ments in data sharing and increased collaboration between aca-demic and industry researchers, clinicians, people living with rare diseases and regulatory agencies9–14. Simultaneously, advances in understanding of disease biology and progress with diagnostics have led to increases in the number of potentially druggable targets and growing recognition of people with potentially treatable disorders15.
The current drug development model for rare diseases often starts with gathering information on a disease and identifying a potential therapeutic target for it. Therapeutic candidates progress to preclini-cal studies and then to clinical trials, with those that are successful in these studies being submitted to regulatory agencies and assessed by health technology assessment agencies and payers before they reach clinical application16. This model has resulted in the approval of mul-tiple drugs from well-established therapeutic modalities such as small molecules and recombinant proteins, as well as a growing number of oligonucleotide therapies, gene therapies and cell therapies17.
Although this model for developing a therapy for people with a specific rare disease exists for good reasons, it is often not viable for developing therapeutics for very small populations (sometimes just individuals), even if some of these individuals could benefit from the same type of therapies. This is especially true given the emergence of genetically targeted therapeutic modalities such as oligonucleotide therapies and genome editing therapies that can be very precise in their action, such that the target population may be as small as one or a few individuals. In such cases, a new development model is needed (Fig. 1). Notably, developing a treatment for a single individual — an ‘N-of-1 therapy’ — has already been shown to be feasible. One of the best-known examples is the development of an oligonucleotide therapy known as milasen for a child with CLN7-related Batten disease18.
In this Review, after defining N-of-1 therapy, we discuss the state-of-the-art of N-of-1 therapy development, highlighting examples of N-of-1 therapies based on different therapeutic modalities. We then con-sider the multiple aspects involved in developing N-of-1 therapies and propose a roadmap for such efforts. We also discuss some of the key challenges for N-of-1 approaches and how they might be addressed.
Definition of N-of-1 therapy In the context of this Review, we define an N-of-1 approach as an individ-ualized therapy developed for and used by one or very few people living with a rare disease. This definition, as such, focuses on an individualized Nature Reviews Drug Discovery Review article initiative for a 6-year-old girl with CLN7 Batten disease (a subtype of neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis)18. A few months after the clinical diag-nosis of Batten disease was made in 2016, whole-genome sequencing enabled the identification of a unique pathogenic variant that induced cryptic splicing of MFSD8 (the gene mutated in CLN7 Batten disease), which was predicted to result in premature translation termination.
An ASO was developed to block cryptic splicing induced by this pathogenic variant. Preclinical studies in patient-derived cells showed that the ASO could restore normal MFSD8 splicing patterns and rescue lysosomal function, and rat studies demonstrated mammalian safety18. After ethical review and manufacture of a clinical-grade lot of this ASO (named milasen, after the patient), intrathecal clinical administration was accepted under a US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) Inves-tigational New Drug (IND) application in 2018, less than 12 months after the variant was detected. It was reported that the treatment sig-nificantly reduced the patient’s number of seizures and improved her quality of life18, but it could not undo the neurological damage already accumulated at the time of administration, and the patient passed away in 2021. This effort showed that individualized therapy development is possible, and inspired other genetic N-of-1 treatment initiatives (Box 1).
This case also illustrates how the development of genetic N-of-1 therapies can use information from therapies developed for larger patient populations. In the case of milasen, the previous development of nusinersen (Spinraza; Ionis Pharmaceuticals/Biogen) for spinal muscular atrophy provided a useful template, as it established that an ASO with the same mechanism of action (modulation of mRNA splicing) and chemistry (RNA with a phosphorothioate backbone and 2′-O-methoxyethyl modifications) could be delivered by intrathecal injections, and was well tolerated. Nusinersen treatment resulted in significant benefit for patients with spinal muscular atrophy type 1 and type 2, especially when treatment was initiated before the onset of symptoms30, leading to its approval by the FDA in 2016. By employing the same chemistry, mechanism of action, formulation and method of delivery as nusinersen (but a different target sequence), milasen’s developers benefitted from prior knowledge about ASOs that modulate mRNA splicing as a platform, allowing the process to be accelerated.
In parallel, Ionis Pharmaceuticals, Neil Shneider from Columbia University Irving Medical Center and Robert Brown from UMass Chan Medical School were developing an ASO for FUS-related amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). This rare genetic form of ALS occurs in fewer than 1% of all cases of ALS. Ionis identified several ASO candidates that could degrade FUS mRNA and that were well tolerated in rodents31,32. These data were shared with Neil Shneider, who selected a lead clinical candidate based on safety and cross-reactivity to rodents and initiated an IND-enabling rodent toxicology study and subsequent treatment in a single individual with advanced-stage ALS in close collaboration with Project ALS. The ASO, initially dubbed jacifusen, appeared to result in a slower disease trajectory before the patient died33. Since then, additional individuals with FUS-related ALS have been treated, and after encouraging results, a clinical trial with this ASO, now offi-cially named ulfnersen, is ongoing in FUS-related ALS, with Ionis Pharmaceuticals as the sponsor34. This example showcases that, sometimes, a treatment can be developed initially for an individual, but with the help of patient organizations can have the potential for treatment of larger groups of patients, supported by corresponding commercial interest.
Another example where an ASO developed for an individual was found to be applicable for further patients is atipeksen, which targets a cryptic splicing variant in the ATM gene that causes ataxia telangiectasia35. The first person with this variant was identified in the United States and has been treated for a number of years. A second person with the same variant was identified in Germany and the fact that an ASO was already available became clear after a cross-referencing effort within the N = 1 Collaborative (N1C). Nature Reviews Drug Discovery Review article the United States, but the individual returned to Tübingen, Germany, where treatment has successfully continued for more than 2 years36.
Gene and cell therapy Gene and cell therapy approaches are ideally suited to treat rare dis-eases caused by pathogenic genetic variants that result in an absent or incorrectly synthesized protein. Currently, targeted gene correc-tion can be achieved through delivery of a functional version of the gene (transgene) inserted in an engineered vector (that is, addition) or through the use of genome editing technologies such as CRISPR–Cas9-based approaches (that is, correction)37. Several approved gene thera-pies for rare diseases use adeno-associated viral (AAV) vectors for in vivo delivery (Fig. 2) or lentiviral vectors for ex vivo cellular modification to deliver the transgenes that encode the protein that needs to be pro-duced to treat the disease38. Genome editing approaches can also be used to disrupt the function of a gene.
Experiences with approved vector-based gene therapies can, in principle, accelerate the development of novel individual products; for instance, if the goal is to express a transgene in the same tissue as an approved gene therapy and the same route of administration can be used, the same vector (or other relevant technology) and promoter sequences could be used, so the new product would only differ in the genetic material that is delivered or the gene sequence that is edited. As such, a platform-like approach can be envisioned to develop gene therapies for diseases that affect very small groups of people.

Antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) therapies can reduce the production of pathogenic proteins by degrading the mRNA coding for them, or restore the production of a functional version of a protein that would otherwise be missing by modulating mRNA splicing. Gene therapies, such as those based on adeno-associated viral (AAV) vectors, can introduce a functional copy of the gene into cells to restore production of a missing protein. Administration of recombinant proteins can compensate for a defective or missing protein. Cell therapies can be based on transplanted cells that carry a functional copy of a gene; the example shown illustrates an individualized cell therapy produced by extracting cells from the patient, modifying them with a viral vector containing a gene that codes for the protein needed for therapeutic function and then readministering them to the patient. Small-molecule drugs can ameliorate diseases caused by protein misfolding or mislocalization, as exemplified by potentiators (shown) and correctors (not shown) used to treat cystic fibrosis by rescuing the function of the defective ion channel. In addition, although not shown, personalized cancer vaccines can also be used as an N-of-1 therapeutic strategy, which involves training the immune system to target antigens that are expressed on the cancer cells of an individual.
Nature Reviews Drug Discovery Review article The Platform Vector Gene Therapies (PaVe-GT) programme aims to test whether using the same AAV manufacturing methods as a platform for multiple rare disease gene therapies can increase the efficiency of clinical trial start-up39. This programme intends to make study results and regulatory records publicly available to ensure knowledge sharing and informing future gene therapy clinical trials for very rare diseases40.
Although the rare disease gene therapies being developed based on such platforms will not typically be true N-of-1 cases, the development of N-of-1 therapies can benefit from the strategy of leveraging existing product designs to streamline development and the regulatory path-way. Examples where gene therapy was developed for very small groups of people with rare diseases include spastic paraplegia 50 (SPG50) and Tay–Sachs disease41,42, as well as a private effort to develop a very spe-cific vector-based treatment for Duchenne muscular dystrophy. This effort was sponsored by Cure Rare Disease, a not-for-profit organization that aims to develop treatments for rare neuromuscular diseases. For a person with Duchenne muscular dystrophy caused by deletion of the muscle promoter for dystrophin, they developed an individualized treatment aiming to upregulate the production of another full-length dystrophin isoform that had been shown to be able to compensate for lack of muscle dystrophin in other individuals43. Although this approach was widely reported to employ CRISPR-based technology, no genome editing was involved; rather, CRISPR-based tech­ nology was used to alter the epigenetic status of the target gene to promote its expression. The editing components were delivered to the patient using AAV9 at high doses. However, the patient — 27 years old with pre-existing respiratory failure — passed away shortly after the treatment due to an innate immune response to the viral vector that led to acute respiratory distress syndrome43.
Genetically modified cell therapies have been used for rare cancers and immune deficiency diseases44–46. Such therapies can be autolo-gous (derived from the patient’s own cells) or allogeneic. Genetically modified autologous cell therapies that are currently marketed are engineered via transduction of the harvested autologous cells with a viral vector (for example, a lentiviral vector) or through genome editing (for example with CRISPR–Cas9 technology) to produce the needed genetic modification; the modified cells are then administered back to the individual to generate the desired treatment effects. An example of such a therapy for rare diseases is Strimvelis, the first approved ex vivo stem cell gene therapy, for the treatment of adenosine deaminase (ADA)‐deficient severe combined immunodeficiency47. This disease is severe and life-threatening, characterized by lymphopenia, fail-ure to thrive and recurrent infections, often leading to fatality within the child’s first years of life48. Strimvelis comprises a single infusion of autologous haematopoietic stem cells that have been genetically modified with a gamma-retroviral vector to introduce a functional copy of the ADA gene.
Unlike other types of gene therapies, genome editing technologies aim to edit the human genome in the somatic cells of the affected individ-uals. Recently, the first therapy that uses genome editing technology — the CRISPR-based therapy exagamglogene autotemcel (Casgevy; CRISPR Therapeutics/Vertex) — was approved by the Medicines and Box 1 | Initiatives working on N-of-1 therapies In the last few years, several networks, not-for-profit organizations and companies have been set up with a focus on creating N-of-1 therapies, although the details of their goals and geographical focus differ. We discuss a few prominent examples here, but this list is not exhaustive.
The international N = 1 Collaborative (N1C) aims to make individualized medicines safe and rapidly accessible to people living with a rare disease worldwide. Primarily focused on antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs), and partially derived from the N-of-1 Task Force of the Oligonucleotide Therapeutics Society, the collaborative brings together clinician-scientists, researchers, people living with a rare disease and companies who are committed to opening up the field of individualized medicines. The hope is that the tools and processes developed can later be adopted by other individualized treatment approaches such as genome editing.
The US-based n-Lorem Foundation aims to apply ASO technology’s efficiency, versatility and specificity to provide experimental ASOs to charitably treat people with a single genetic variant that affects fewer than 30 people with the same variant worldwide116. In less than 5 years, n-Lorem has built a pipeline of more than 90 target genes, filed 13 Investigational New Drug (INDs) applications with the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and initiated treatment of 8 patients, with the treatment of a further 3 patients to be initiated in the next few months.
The 1 Mutation 1 Medicine (1M1M) initiative aims to create a scalable European platform for developing and implementing variant-specific ASO treatments for individuals with nano-rare neurological diseases96. In order to do so, a core–periphery multi-stakeholder network has been formed that brings together academic, patient and industry organizations to select potential cases for N-of-1 therapy development, develop ASOs and treat individuals.
Similarly, the Bespoke Gene Therapy Consortium (BGTC) brings together industrial partners, not-for-profit organizations and two government organizations, the FDA and the National Institutes of Health (NIH), with the aim to develop platforms and standards to speed the development and delivery of customized or ‘bespoke’ adeno-associated viral (AAV)-based gene addition therapies117 ,118.
Cure Rare Disease is a non-profit biotech focused on the development of gene editing, replacement and ASO approaches for neuromuscular diseases through academic collaborations and embedding translational expertise.
To facilitate platform development, the Access to Gene Therapies fOr RAre disease (AGORA) consortium is developing and sharing processes and protocols119. This platform aims to tackle the growing economic hurdles that prevent gene therapies from reaching children with ultra-rare diseases.
Finally, in 2023, the International Rare Diseases Research Consortium (IRDiRC) set up a Task Force to prepare for genetic N-of-1 treatments of patients with ultra-rare variants. The overall objective of this Task Force is to connect different N-of-1 efforts to reduce duplication, achieve global consensus and create a roadmap towards development and implementation of N-of-1 treatment, including producing this reference document summarizing the current state-of-the-art, to raise awareness of the N-of-1 concepts and challenges with all stakeholders.

Non-viral ex vivo CRISPR-based edit-ing of haemopoietic stem cells from the patient is used to knockout a repressive function of BCL11A and thereby reactivate fetal haemoglobin synthesis, and the modified cells are then administered to the patient48.
Clinical trials are ongoing to evaluate genome editing therapies for other rare diseases including transthyretin amyloidosis, heredi-tary angioedema and severe familial hypercholesterolaemia51–54. In parallel, research is ongoing to develop genome editing for N-of-1 applications. This technology can correct disease-causing variants directly at the DNA level, allowing greater precision than integrating viral approaches, and, importantly, correction in the native context retains cell type-specific gene expression55,56. The additional chal-lenge here compared with the cases applying ASO and AAV-based therapies highlighted above is that data for approved and thoroughly tested therapies are more limited. However, collaborative efforts where protocols and processes are shared have been established, such as the Somatic Cell Genome Editing programme at the National Institutes of Health (NIH)57,58.
Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapies are another type of individualized cell therapy59,60. Their production involves collecting the patient’s T cells and genetically engineering them with viral vectors to express CARs that can recognize and bind to tumour antigens such as CD19 and BCMA61. Once modified, the T cells are multiplied in the labo-ratory and reintroduced into the patient. Ideally, these CAR-T cells pro-liferate within the patient and target cancer cells bearing the specific antigen. Since 2017, several CAR-T cell therapies have been approved by the FDA for the treatment of blood cancers, including lymphomas, some forms of leukaemia and, most recently, multiple myeloma62–65. However, although such therapies are individualized because the cells are specific to each patient, the modification is the same for a given cell therapy product (for example, introduction of a CAR encoding CD19) and they can be tested in trials involving multiple patients with the same type of cancer using the same (often established) clinical end-points. Their development therefore does not face all of the challenges of the other N-of-1 therapies discussed above.
Personalized cancer vaccines Genetic instability is a hallmark of tumours66. Mutations in cancer cells can lead to the expression of tumour-specific neoantigens, with the majority of these being unique to a single person67. These neoantigens can be used to develop personalized therapeutic cancer vaccines that trigger a broad-based antitumour immune response yet are specific for the tumour of an individual. This field has seen a surge of activity in recent years based on technological advances in different therapeutic modalities and improved understanding of tumour biology68,69.
The first step in the development of neoantigen vaccines is the use of next-generation sequencing of both the tumour biopsy and healthy tissue68,70 to identify tumour-specific variants, which are then evaluated for their capacity to produce an immune response. Different therapeutic platforms for developing vaccines based on such variants are advancing, including peptides, dendritic cells, DNA, RNA and viral vectors. One example is mRNA vaccines that encode tumour antigens, which can result in adaptive immune responses and antitumour effects and have the benefit of relatively low cost and rapid development. Importantly from an evidence generation and data extrapolation per-spective, most of the components of medicinal products from these platforms are similar for each person.
Multiple personalized vaccine candidates targeting between 5 and 50 different neoantigens70 are now in clinical development for cancers such as melanoma and pancreatic carcinoma71. These early-phase clinical trials have shown safety and feasibility, and also the first proof of efficacy72–76. As with the CAR-T cell products high-lighted above, however, these personalized vaccines can be tested in clinical trials involving multiple patients with the same cancer type using the same clinical end-points, and so they face fewer and differ-ent challenges in their development compared with other types of N-of-1 therapies.
Small-molecule drugs Cystic fibrosis is a rare disease caused by pathogenic variants that negatively affect the function of a protein called cystic fibrosis trans-membrane conductance regulator (CFTR) that functions as a chloride channel. In the past decade or so, several small-molecule CFTR modu-lators have been approved to treat cystic fibrosis, and although they were not developed as N-of-1 therapies, they have since been applied in N-of-1 settings.
Approved CFTR modulators fall into two classes: potentiators such as ivacaftor that bind to the defective ion channel and potentiate its function (Fig. 2); and correctors such as lumacaftor, elexacaftor and tezacaftor that correct protein folding and trafficking defects, thus increasing plasma membrane insertion and function of the channel. Ultimately, both drug classes increase CFTR function in patients with cystic fibrosis77. Importantly, the optimal drug (or drug combina-tion) depends on whether the pathogenic variant(s) that a particu-lar patient has primarily affects CFTR misfolding/mistrafficking or channel opening.
So far, ~2,000 variants that cause cystic fibrosis have been identified78. Ivacaftor, the first CFTR modulator to be approved, in 2012, was initially developed for patients who have a G551D mutation in CFTR, which is present in 4–5% of patients79. Since then, the devel-opment and approval of small-molecule correctors has expanded the treatable patient population: the combination of elexacaftor, tezacaftor and ivacaftor can be used to treat ~90% of all people with cystic fibrosis77.
However, there are still some patients with very rare disease- causing mutations that have not been included in the clinical trials for these products. In a landmark move in 2017, the FDA expanded the approved indication of ivacaftor from 10 mutations to 33 mutations, based in part on in vitro results, rather than requiring new clinical safety and efficacy data80. Other next-generation therapies for cystic fibrosis are in development81.
Although CFTR modulators are approved for use according to genotype, there is a heterogeneous response in people with cystic fibrosis with the same genotype, meaning that an N-of-1 precision medicine approach of theratyping (matching therapies with specific variants) using innovative technology is needed. One such example is the use of ‘CF avatars’, which are individual patient-derived organoids that can be used to predict response82. Conversely, these modulators have demonstrated that some people with very rare variants that are not covered by the approved indication can respond to treatment, but there may not be a third-party payor-supported pathway to access treatment83. Currently, the CFTR modulators are the only small mol-ecules that are used in an N-of-1 setting, where preclinical research is done to assess whether they could be beneficial for patients with pathogenic variants other than the variant(s) for which the modulator was originally developed.
Nature Reviews Drug Discovery Review article Roadmap for N-of-1 treatment development It is clear that N-of-1 therapy development cannot use the traditional drug development pathway. However, it is also clear that the devel-opment of N-of-1 treatments cannot operate in a regulatory and commercial vacuum. It is against this background that we have estab-lished a roadmap and framework for these therapies to support timely development and clinical implementation (Fig. 3).
This roadmap sets out the stages involved in bringing an N-of-1 ther-apy to patients and includes the different approaches and the tools that might support those aiming to do so (Table 1). It also includes consid-erations at each stage, and the stakeholders and organizations that are connected (Fig. 4). With N-of-1 therapy currently at the border between research and therapy, the tools and processes of the roadmap can be optimized as each case and the associated data on safety and efficacy of therapeutic candidates are shared. As such, it should be considered a living document that can be built on and strengthened over time.

During most of the stages and processes of the roadmap, there are ethical issues and concerns related to equity, possible risk versus possible benefit and uncertainty. Rather than making a special sec-tion on ethics19, we have woven these issues into each of the sections below. Furthermore, it is important that developers of individualized treatments operate within the regulations of their own regulatory jurisdiction (Box 2).
A practical example of a pilot project pulling together the different elements from diagnosis to treatment to monitoring in a new develop-ment pathway is the UK’s Rare Therapies Launch Pad (RTLP)84. This initiative was formally announced in autumn 2023 and aims, through multi-stakeholder collaboration, to build the necessary infrastructure to make individualized medicines accessible, scalable and sustainable. Key components include developing a visible route for diagnosed patients to link to a treatment modality, underpinned by a propor-tionate regulatory framework and patient monitoring with iterative learning in the real world. A commentary presenting the principles of the pathway will be published in the near future by the RTLP.
Identification of eligible people living with a rare disease Genetic diagnosis and assessment of treatment amenability. Regardless of the specific therapeutic modality, there are several aspects that relate to all individualized therapy developments. The first is the correct identification of eligible people living with a rare disease. Currently, this typically begins with a person presenting to the healthcare system, being appropriately recognized by a healthcare professional as an individual with a rare disease and then being referred to an expert centre or clinical research network. Even with appropriate referral, diagnosis of rare diseases is often challenging in terms of the time taken to recognize the need for detailed analysis, the availability of or access to diagnostic testing and the proper interpretation of results to arrive at the correct diagnosis85–87.
A second route to the identification of eligible people for N-of-1 therapy are several programmes that have been initiated in recent years that could systematically help provide a diagnosis for people with a rare disease as early as possible, potentially even before symptoms develop, by applying population-based whole-genome screening or newborn screening88–90. With increased application of diagnostic and genetic analysis tools, it is expected that more eligible patients will be identified. However, a current challenge is that it may not be clear to those diagnosing the patients whether or not they have a type of disease (for example, owing to a particular genetic variant) for which a potential therapy is already available or could be developed through an N-of-1 approach. Software tools to flag actionable genetic variants need to be developed. These software tools could be particularly valuable for rapidly progressing severe diseases that begin early in life, for which preventing loss of function as early as possible is crucial for long-term outcomes.
From an ethical perspective, there are inequities in access to healthcare systems within and between regions to obtain a correct diagnosis, which then also have an impact on assessment of eligibility for (individualized) treatments. For example, these inequities are due to the lack of detailed standardized diagnostic criteria, for which avail-ability varies from region to region91, or due to the costs of obtaining a diagnosis92.
Assessment of eligibility for N-of-1 therapy. Once a person is diag-nosed with a rare disease, whether there are currently available thera-pies suitable for them needs to be assessed. If not, consideration could be given to whether developing an N-of-1 therapy may be a possibility.
Many factors are involved in this consideration, including the gene and specific pathogenic variants found in the individual, the mecha-nism of disease and the organ or organs involved. For instance, current experience with ASOs shows that these products can be efficiently delivered to the liver, the central nervous system and the eye in humans93,94, which means that new N-of-1 therapies with ASOs can be considered to treat diseases for which product delivery to these tissues is needed. However, native ASO delivery to muscle is poor. So, a person with a genetic variant causing a muscle disease would be a poor candidate for development of an N-of-1 ASO therapy at present, even if, in principle, their disease is molecularly amenable based on the nature of the variant itself, until better mechanisms for delivery are demonstrated to be effective in humans, such as the transferrin receptor–antibody conjugates that are currently being tested in clinical trials for Duchenne muscular dystrophy and myotonic dystrophy95.
In cases in which a person qualifies based on these eligibility cri-teria, it needs to be assessed at an individual level whether they would be expected to benefit from such a therapy96. For example, if lack of a protein leads to developmental problems during embryogenesis, resulting in structural malformations at birth, restoring the missing protein postnatally will not correct the malformations.
