It is also crucial to have discussions about what risk–benefit trade-offs such individuals would find appropriate. Institutional ethics committees and others charged with evaluating the ethics of proposed interventions would be best served by understanding how individuals similar to the patient would evaluate a possible side effect or a possible beneficial outcome.
Another eligibility criterion is that a multidisciplinary care team for the specific rare disease can be established to look after the patient while the individualized therapy is being developed, as well as during the administration period. These multidisciplinary care teams, which are already common in oncology, comprise specialists in areas such as oncology (medical, surgical, radiation), pathology, radiology and nursing. The principle of these multidisciplinary care teams ensures that comprehensive healthcare according to established standards is provided following timely diagnosis, and that all is in place for therapy initiation and monitoring once an N-of-1 therapy option becomes available97–99.
A further eligibility criterion is that the healthcare system needs to be willing to accept responsibility for the patient within their local policy framework in order to proceed towards potential treatment readiness. In this phase, not only the healthcare provider but also the healthcare system and the hospital should be able to implement the N-of-1 approach. Important factors to be considered include an evaluation by the healthcare system of the overall cost of care, includ-ing the cost and process for the development of the N-of-1 therapy and the costs related to continuous treatment and monitoring where applicable. At present, N-of-1 therapies cost millions of dollars and, in the United States, are not covered by most payers because they are considered experimental. There are therefore immediate equity con-cerns about who may have access. In Europe, patients can be treated on a named patient basis, which involves less administrative burden. So far, costs have been absorbed by hospitals where patients are treated, but this is not a scalable solution. A dialogue has been initiated with payers in Europe by European N-of-1 researchers, but the common feedback is that data to show efficacy in several patients are needed before a concrete discussion can start100.
Box 2 | The regulatory context for N-of-1 therapies Different geographic jurisdictions have varying requirements for N-of-1 therapy development. In the United States, treatment with novel investigational therapies can only be initiated after opening with the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) an Investigational New Drug (IND) application containing information on product design, manufacturing, and in vitro and non-clinical toxicology testing, as well as a proposed clinical protocol for the first-in-human study. An IND application can be opened for the purpose of product development or for the purpose of clinical treatment through expanded access to investigational therapies120,121. The FDA’s review of the IND application package ensures that the information regarding product manufacturing is sufficient to support use of a quality investigational product in humans and that data from preclinical studies as well as the design of clinical investigations provide reasonable assurance of safety before the treatment is given to one or more individuals.
In March 2020, the FDA held a workshop on facilitating development of individualized therapeutics and has since been open to receiving IND applications for therapies developed for very small populations of patients with rare diseases as well as individual patients, with the ability to leverage previously collected non-clinical and manufacturing information by cross-referencing available data between INDs122. To transition the regular product development pathway to new approaches that would fit the purpose and promote future development of individualized therapies, the FDA has published a guidance for N-of-1 antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) development and issued a notice soliciting input from stakeholders on the challenges and opportunities for the development of individualized gene and cell therapies123,124. Under the provisions of the Food and Drug Omnibus Reform Act of 2022, the FDA created additional regulatory incentives for the development of platform technologies to enable leveraging significant efficiencies in product development, manufacturing and regulatory review to reduce time and expenditures in product development, including development of individualized therapeutics125. The draft guidance explaining the platform technology designation programme was published by the FDA in May 2024 (ref. 126).
In the European Union, people living with rare diseases can be treated on a named patient basis with unlicensed medicines, where clinicians take full responsibility and approval may only be needed from local or national Institutional Review Boards, as specified in European Directive 2001/83/EC Article 5 or individual member states’ requirements127 ,128. Notably, regulations for initiating treatment with experimental compounds on a named patient basis differ across European countries. Named patient treatment is administered as patient care and there is no goal of obtaining marketing authorization with the competent authorities. Nevertheless, the European Medicines Agency (EMA) has been willing to advise on the development of N-of-1 ASO development through its scientific advice procedure96.
A similar approach is taken in Australia for phase I studies with ASOs, but the pathways are more challenging for cell and gene therapies. They are reviewed by competent authorities depending on how the cell and gene therapy is administered. For example, chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy, which involves ex vivo manipulation of lymphocytes, is classified as a Class 4 biological, which renders it unsuitable for evaluation by the Pharmaceutical Benefit Advisory Committee129. However, therapies directly administered to a patient are classified as prescription medicines and are evaluated by the Pharmaceutical Benefit Advisory Committee.
In Canada, similar to the United States, an N-of-1 treatment can be initiated after Health Canada authorizes a Clinical Trial Application. Currently, Health Canada does not have specific guidance for N-of-1 therapies. However, in 2017, Health Canada launched the Regulatory Review of Drugs and Devices initiative, with the goal of having a regulatory system that provides greater and faster access to therapeutic products that are better aligned with healthcare system needs, including drugs for rare diseases130,131.
Nature Reviews Drug Discovery Review article Communication with the patient and family/caregivers. After these eligibility checks have been completed, the person living with the rare disease (and/or the surrogate decision-maker) should be informed about the possibility of an unproven N-of-1 therapy for their condition, and interest in such an experimental approach should be assessed. These assessments are not conversations at a single point in time but are, ideally, extended discussions, giving the person (when feasible), their families/caregivers and others involved in decision-making (as well as the scientific team) the opportunity to evaluate and re-evaluate over time the possible benefits and risks of N-of-1 treatment versus the impact of the disease itself. What is perceived as benefit, as well as the tolerance for risk and uncertainty, may vary between people with the same disease and across cultures.
Depending on the therapeutic modality that will be used, the N-of-1 therapy to be developed could be considered for a single administra-tion for certain gene therapies or repeat administration for most other therapies. When a therapy involves ongoing treatment administration, it will be important to discuss the start and stop criteria with the patient and family/caregivers before treatment initiation, and at the same time to reflect whether the treatment effects and burdens are as expected and whether the start/stop criteria that were initially established need to be adjusted. It will be important to have an independent monitor-ing board, as the researcher/clinician may not be able to objectively view the case because of their investment in developing a treatment and/or the potential consequences of a successful individualized treatment with regards to publications and career progression.
Despite strong scientific rationale and extrapolation of existing data, individualized treatment still involves a high amount of uncer-tainty. There is no guarantee that the intervention will be as effective or safe as initially hoped, but nonetheless the risks of not intervening are usually clear (with progressive diseases, things will get worse). This puts extra challenges on patients and their families/caregivers, especially for some treatments that are intended for single adminis-tration based on the expectation of long-term effects, but which can also have long-term implications. For example, although it may be desirable owing to waning efficacy, further administrations of a gene therapy based on the same viral vector (either the original therapy or a subsequently developed therapy that could be more effective) may not be possible owing to an immune response to the vector.
At the same time, some patients and their families/caregivers have expectations that might not be commensurate with the likely treatment effect (for example, an expectation that it may bring back function that is irreversibly lost). This may complicate decision-making and may lead to patients and their families taking undue risks based on unrealistic expectations of the potential magnitude of benefit. As such, as soon as a patient and/or their family expresses interest in the pursuit of an N-of-1 therapy, psychological support should be provided and an ongoing dialogue should start to allow the patient and their family time to make a decision that is as informed as possible, given the inherent uncertainties and risks of side effects.
Development of the therapy and preclinical evaluation Choice of modality. As described earlier, there are numerous therapeu-tic approaches that can be individualized for eligible patients. Which one to select depends on the characteristics of the disease, as the individual-ized therapy needs to build on available data for an approved approach, as illustrated by the milasen example. Furthermore, selection depends on the pathogenic variant, the gene, the pathological mechanism and whether the therapies work in dividing or non-dividing cells.
When a disease is caused by a toxic gain of function of a gene, ASOs and small interfering RNAs are approved modalities that can address this at a genetic level by promoting the degradation of the mRNA, and genome editing therapies to knockout the target gene are in clinical trials. When a disease is caused by a loss of protein function, sometimes there is a choice between gene therapies based on viral vectors and ASOs, but sometimes there is not; for example, when the gene is very large and a replacement copy exceeds the viral vector capacity, ASOs may be the only option. There are also cases when there are multiple options. For example, in the milasen case, the patient’s disease was the result of lack of functioning MFSD8. Gene replacement therapy using a viral vector has been contemplated as an option to restore protein production in the central nervous system, but an ASO approach was selected because its development could be expedited more quickly and with lower costs than a gene therapy approach.
Evaluation of treatment efficacy in model systems. Preclinical devel-opment for individualized treatments is particularly time sensitive when dealing with progressive diseases. Therefore, a balance has to be struck between establishing that the N-of-1 therapy is sufficiently likely to be effective and safe and ensuring that treatment can be initiated while the person receiving it is still in a relevant treatment window. For proof-of-concept studies, in vitro patient-derived cell models may often suffice, but animal studies may be needed in some cases96. The choice and sufficiency of non-clinical evidence will largely depend on the demonstrated biological activity of any given product and the anticipated risks of the therapeutic strategy. Ideally, effects should be shown not only on relevant gene transcripts but also on proteins, and, if possible, on pathological features of the disease.
Manufacturing of the therapy for clinical use. The N-of-1 therapy needs to be produced to high-quality standards. The criteria for this good manufacturing practice (GMP or GMP-like101,102) varies depend-ing on the modality and jurisdiction. However, obvious criteria that always apply are sufficient purity, sterility and lack of endotoxins. Furthermore, the product’s biological effects suggesting efficacy should be confirmed at a molecular level in an in vitro model system before treating the patient.
The funding model for individualized therapy development and manufacturing is currently a large hurdle, and innovative payment and reimbursement approaches are urgently needed. The need for specific sustainable funding models is discussed in the ‘Outlook’ section.
Safety assessment. N-of-1 therapies build on data that are available for approved treatments of the same modality for larger groups of patients. This means some information is already available on expected tolerability and safety. However, the individualized treatment will not be identical and the specific condition to be treated will be different. As such, preclinical safety studies for the individualized treatment remain important for N-of-1 drug development.
The exact nature and scope of these preclinical studies may vary widely depending on the clinical context, therapeutic modalities and regional regulatory requirements (Box 2). For example, for gene and cell therapies and cancer vaccines, long-term safety and efficacy data will need to be collected after treatment with monitoring for latent adverse events that may manifest later in life, and so there should be systems put in place for collection of these data96.
It is anticipated that regulatory requirements for different prod-uct categories in different countries and jurisdictions will evolve as Nature Reviews Drug Discovery Review article experience with product modalities and N-of-1 development builds, and additional tools such as surrogate in vitro or in silico studies and simulation become available.
Evaluation of the effects of the therapy Selection of clinical outcome measures with sufficient signal-to-noise ratio on a single-subject level. It can be challenging to show clinical efficacy in clinical trials in small populations, with N-of-1 treat-ment being the most extreme challenge. Nonetheless, several options exist to tackle this challenge. To detect meaningful clinical change, a treated subject’s disease course can be compared intra-individually (for example, with the progression of the patient’s disease course prior to treatment) or inter-individually, with a cohort of (historical or concurrent) controls with the same or sufficiently similar disease manifestations96. In specialized cases, additional comparisons can be contemplated, such as comparing vision in one eye receiving a targeted therapy versus the contralateral eye which may be left untreated, or employing in silico digital avatars as synthetic controls.
The selection of outcome measures is of critical importance in N-of-1 studies. In particular, the outcome measures or instruments should capture disease manifestations that are acceptable to the expert disease clinical community and meaningful to the patient (when feasible) and/or family, and thus selection should be done with the patient and their family. For instance, for neurological conditions, families often prioritize the achievement of physical and cognitive developmental milestones, and/or the ability to maintain an age-appropriate function-ing level, both of which are examples of very meaningful and acceptable measures of clinical efficacy in paediatric rare diseases where delays in physical and cognitive abilities are the main disease manifestations96. Capturing patient-reported outcome measures can also add value to monitoring patient benefit. Moreover, assessments that allow effi-cacy outcomes to be measured frequently or continually over time rather than at single time points might increase the signal-to-noise ratio. For example, it has been shown that, even at an N-of-1 level, con-tinuous capture of digital-motor outcomes by body-worn sensors in day-to-day life as opposed to one-time laboratory-based capture might substantially increase the ability to detect meaningful changes103.
To allow comparison of the disease course before and after treat-ment initiation, data capture before, during and after the treatment will be critical. Given the unique setting of individualized treatment, and individualized outcome measures, a new type of collective registry could be built that allows the flexibility required to properly individual-ize the registry for each person living with a rare disease, which can then be used to monitor multiple individualized therapies for each person. At the same time, the treated person would be included in disease registries to allow comparison with natural history data. Comparison with natural history in the context of N-of-1 therapies can come with some challenges. First, natural history data are not available for every rare disease. Furthermore, the natural history of a disease can involve very variable trajectories, and potentially the course of the disease of an individual with a specific rare variant could deviate from the natural history observed for previous patients with the same disease, but with different variants. An example of this issue is seen with ataxia telangi-ectasia, for which there are different disease trajectories for different mutation types104.
However, as the primary intention of therapy is patient benefit, not the generation of generalizable data, there will need to be clear policies about data ownership, privacy and confidentiality, and to what extent patients may or may not decline to participate in data collection activities. These data are of immense societal and scientific importance as they will, on aggregate, enable much broader under-standing of genetic medicine; however, the data cannot be collected from unknowing or unwilling patients.
Selection of molecular outcome measures. Given the potential for long latency until clinical outcomes show robust efficacy, as well as the inherent variation in clinical outcomes due to external factors, the clinical outcomes should ideally be complemented by molecular pharmacodynamic outcomes, which might capture a treatment response earlier. For example, detection of protein restoration in cerebrospinal fluid or blood shows a pharmacodynamic effect at a molecular level for proteins that are released by neurons96. In cystic fibrosis, the use of the sweat test as a biomarker of correction of the underlying defect of the chloride channel is a direct measure of efficacy in an individual.
Treatment readiness, management and monitoring on a single- subject level. All of the tools and processes and the individualized therapy come together at the point when the person living with the rare disease receives the therapy. For certain gene and cell therapies, treatment may involve a single product administration with long-term monitoring for safety and efficacy. As mentioned before, tools to cap-ture data and legally and ethically compliant plans to store and share the data need to be in place before starting the treatment.
For therapies involving multiple treatments, the dose can be modi-fied over time, with safety and efficacy monitoring and discussions with the patient and the family guiding increases, caps or decreases in the dose. Also, the data collection is crucial to guide the clinician. Nota-bly, monitoring is necessary for as long as the treatment is provided to the patient, and it is important that the clinician, patient and their family/caregivers are aware of this commitment. Eventually, carefully anonymized data sharing with the wider community will be key to support future developments and evidence generation.
Outlook For N-of-1 therapies, every aspect is individualized, from therapy devel-opment to selecting outcome measures on a single-subject level, ensur-ing clinical implementation of the treatment plan in the hospital and establishing start/stop criteria105. Although each individual case is likely to be unique, lessons about aspects such as clinical outcomes, disease biology, tools, therapeutic modalities and treatment plans should be collected from each case and shared whenever possible. This will be crucial to guide future treatment of additional patients who may be identified to be eligible for the same treatment or same therapeutic approach. Furthermore, there are many outstanding ethical questions in this nascent field, with new issues likely to arise from future cases19, and data sharing is the only way to establish an ethical, patient-centric treatment framework.
In the short term, the focus should primarily be on quickly pro-gressing severe and life-threatening diseases, where it will be easier to measure treatment effects in a shorter time frame and where the toler-ance for uncertainty and risk will be higher. However, once individual-ized treatments are more established, results could be extrapolated to also include slower progressive or less severe diseases, where it will take longer to show functional effects, but where the uncertainty will be reduced based on the data from previous development programmes.
Data sharing aspects have to be developed via an evolving frame-work that sets specific standards. Furthermore, with sufficiently similar Nature Reviews Drug Discovery Review article treatments, such as ASOs for brain diseases, general safety and efficacy profiles may become apparent when collating data from multiple individuals and multiple preclinical safety and efficacy studies. How-ever, the field can only learn from these datasets when they are shared transparently. Use of a common dictionary of adverse events (such as MedDRA terminology) within a specific class of drugs or a disease area will provide the basis for a broader understanding of common and rare risks, thereby enabling targeted preclinical and clinical safety model-ling. As such, this might improve safety for future N-of-1 treatments developed based on the same drug or the same therapeutic modal-ity. Furthermore, reporting of specific unsafe treatments will enable reverse translation to see whether there are model systems that could predict the unanticipated side effects to improve safety assessments for future products.
The development of N-of-1 therapies currently comes at substan­ tial financial cost, which raises the key question of how to pay for the development and administration of these therapies. Although the N-of-1 therapy field is quickly developing, such therapies are still at a pioneering stage, with few having been developed in a systematic man-ner. This makes it difficult to determine the extent of the costs involved and how representative they may be in general, as the first attempt for a specific modality will probably be much more expensive than future developments, and costs could be reduced if N-of-1 approaches become more widely applied. For example, GMP production of drug candidates for clinical trials usually has an emphasis on large-scale manufacture of each candidate. However, the manufacture of N-of-1 therapies needs different but very similar products at a smaller scale. Efforts are ongoing for the small-scale GMP production of ASOs; for example, with several partners of the N1C and in Europe in the Medicine Made to Measure (MMM) doctoral training network. When the demand for small-batch GMP manufacturing increases, commercial efforts to provide such services could reduce the costs. A first paper on the cost of an individualized therapy has been published, showing that the cost for the development was largely based on preclinical testing, in addition to costs for therapeutic development, clinical care and manufacturing106.
Learning from past developments may allow optimization of the preclinical development process to remove uninformative studies, potentially also reducing costs. For example, if in vivo safety studies in animals are demonstrated to be poorly predictive of human safety, the requirement for them could be removed in the future, also in alignment with the FDA Modernization Act 2.0 and analogous guidelines in Europe to limit the unnecessary use of laboratory animals107,108. Related to this, if reverse translation allows better prediction of human safety from in vitro and/or in vivo safety experiments, these could be streamlined, thus reducing costs. This will depend on ongoing work in the N-of-1 development field and also in orphan drug development more broadly.
Notably, the costs also depend on differences in regulatory requirements in different countries or regions (Box 2); for example, the insistence of the FDA on GMP and good laboratory practice (GLP)-compliant studies compared with the flexibility offered in Europe may increase the costs of N-of-1 development in the United States. A frame-work to determine the typical costs of N-of-1 development and develop a sustainable approach to paying them is needed to enable the develop-ment of the field and the wider implementation of N-of-1 therapies in clinical practice. This framework should include the costs of research to develop the N-of-1 therapy, the production of the N-of-1 therapy, the clinical implementation of treatment delivery and monitoring of the N-of-1 therapy, and other out-of-pocket costs such as overnight stays and sustenance costs for multiday monitoring, or travel to an expert hospital multiple times per year for a patient and caregivers. In this, pricing should be based on the average cost of previous similar development of a specific therapeutic modality, plus an agreed-upon additional margin to further incentivize development106.
To develop models that enable payment for N-of-1 therapies beyond traditional fee-for-service agreements, elements could be taken from discussions around other therapies such as transplantation or gene therapies that have needed to determine what elements con-tribute to a fair pricing, and how to take uncertainty of the outcomes of treatment into account, such as a framework recently developed for paying for gene therapy109. Building on work that will be done in the RTLP110 could hopefully also be possible. Furthermore, debate is ongo-ing in different countries about what are suitable payment models for highly innovative therapies, for which standard payment models are not successful111–113. One potential model that can be considered is the subscription payment model, in which a subscription fee, ideally funded by a payor such as the government or an insurance company, would be directed to a centre of excellence or a (non-)commercial organization. This subscription revenue would allow this academic or (non-)profit centre to sustain ongoing innovation, streamline develop-ment processes and finance critical projects for patients with rapidly advancing disorders106. Another model from which elements can be considered is the pay-for-performance model. Under this model, pay-ments to providers are directly tied to specific performance metrics, such as patient outcomes114. Once N-of-1 therapy development is more established, there may be commercial interest in developing such therapies, whereas commercial interest is currently limited to com-panies providing services, such as GMP production and conducting safety studies.
In conclusion, the field of N-of-1 therapy development is very dynamic, with a continuous need to collaborate and learn from others. Multiple educational tools are available that address different aspects of the field of N-of-1 therapy, and the IRDiRC Task Force has put together an inventory of existing texts, lectures and tools for various therapeutic approaches that may be of help to those embarking on individualized therapy development115. Only by sharing information and openly dis-cussing medical, methodological and ethical successes and failures will the field continue to develop and offer the potential for more people living with ultra-rare diseases to receive an effective and safe therapy.

bedrock_calls.system_prompt:
You are an HTA and Market Access strategist extracting structured evidence from one source document for a JCA (Joint Clinical Assessment) comparator and outcome scoping request.

You will be told the REQUESTED INTERVENTION and the REQUESTED POPULATION. Extract every distinct claim the document makes that is relevant to comparator or outcome scoping.

CRITICAL - DO NOT HALLUCINATE:
- Use ONLY information explicitly stated in the provided text. Never use outside medical knowledge to fill a gap, infer a typical dose, assume a standard comparator, or complete a partial fact with what is usually true.
- If a field is not explicitly stated, its value MUST be an empty string. Never invent a value to avoid leaving something blank.
- Do not paraphrase in a way that adds specificity the text did not have.

FIELD DEFINITIONS - read these; they are not self-evident:

subject_drug: the drug this specific claim is ABOUT - the treatment being assessed, studied or recommended in the passage you are extracting from. A document about a disease often discusses several drugs. If the passage is about a DIFFERENT drug than the requested intervention, say so here. Never write the requested intervention's name unless the passage is genuinely about it.

comparator.as_stated: the treatment this claim names as a comparison, alternative or standard of care - exactly as the source words it, including a regimen's full component list. A drug name, a named regimen, or a legitimate generic category the source states as the most specific thing available ("best supportive care", "physician's choice of chemotherapy"). NOT a sentence, NOT a trial name, NOT a statistical annotation.

comparator.role - choose exactly one:
  "active_comparator"  - studied, recommended or required AS the comparison for the subject drug in the population this passage describes
  "prior_therapy"      - treatment the patient RECEIVED BEFORE reaching this population (e.g. an induction regimen preceding a maintenance-phase question). This is treatment history, NOT a comparator
  "background_therapy" - given to all arms as a backbone, not the thing being compared
  "intervention_arm"   - this IS the subject drug's own arm, not a comparator
  "unclear"            - the passage does not let you tell
Getting this wrong is the single most common error: an induction-phase backbone named near the right population is prior therapy, not a comparator.

comparator.components: for a combination regimen, the complete list of substances AS ONE SOURCE STATES THEM. Never pool components from two different regimens that share an ingredient.

comparator.comparator_scenario - from the source's own language, choose one:
  "unique" (names one comparator) | "each_required" (several, required together) |
  "at_least_one" (several, at least one acceptable) | "individualised" (a bundle of options chosen by patient characteristics)

comparator.retain_all_status: "confirmed_droppable" or "confirmed_must_retain" ONLY when the source itself states a droppability preference. Otherwise "unconfirmed" - which will be the case for the great majority of sources, because this is a procedural preference, not a clinical fact. Never infer it.

DO NOT populate any drug class or mechanism for the comparator. That is resolved downstream from the comparator's own substance identity. If you write a class here it will be the SUBJECT drug's class, which is the exact error this instruction prevents.

population_context.*: the disease/population context THE SOURCE ITSELF states for this claim, in the source's own words - distinct from the requested population, which may be broader or narrower. Fill line_of_therapy, prior_therapy, stage, biomarker and treatment_setting_intent with what THIS passage says, never with the requested population's own label. If the passage states an interval since prior therapy or since relapse, put it in "other".

recommendation_strength (clinical guidelines only): "preferred" | "conditional_alternative" | "not_recommended" | "not_stated", as the guideline itself grades it. Never present a conditional or alternative recommendation as preferred.

outcome.measure: the outcome or endpoint named.
outcome.result: the reported figure, if any, exactly as stated.
outcome.unit: the unit of measurement EXACTLY as the source reports it (e.g. "months, median", "% of patients", "HR (95% CI)") - never invented, never assumed from general knowledge of what a typical unit would be.
outcome.instrument: the named instrument, where the source names one (e.g. a specific questionnaire). Empty otherwise.
outcome.is_requirement: true when the source states this outcome as one an assessment REQUIRES or EXPECTS in scope (an HTA methods document, an assessment scope table, a guideline's stated outcome set). false when the source is merely REPORTING a result for it. These are different things and the distinction matters more than the value.
outcome.requirement_type: "relative_effect_required" | "descriptive_only" | "" - only when the source states it.

evidence_quote: a VERBATIM span copied from the text that contains this claim. It must appear character-for-character in the text. If you cannot copy such a span, omit the whole record rather than paraphrasing.
evidence_locator: where in the document it sits (section heading, table number, page), if the text makes that visible.

member_state: the country whose body/guideline this claim belongs to, when the document is a national source. "EU-wide" for an EU-level record. Empty if unclear.

MULTIPLE POPULATIONS IN ONE DOCUMENT: a document can describe several populations for the same drug. Output SEPARATE records, one per population the text actually describes. Each comparator stays attached to the population it was ACTUALLY reported against - never pulled into the requested population's record just because the same document also discusses that population elsewhere.

Return ONLY a JSON array, no preamble, no markdown fences. Empty array if the document contains nothing relevant:
[
  {"finding_type": "comparator",
   "subject_drug": "...",
   "member_state": "",
   "comparator": {"as_stated": "", "role": "active_comparator", "is_combination": false,
                  "components": [], "comparator_scenario": "", "retain_all_status": "unconfirmed"},
   "population_context": {"disease": "", "subtype_histology": "", "stage": "", "biomarker": "",
                          "line_of_therapy": "", "prior_therapy": "",
                          "treatment_setting_intent": "", "age_band": "", "other": "",
                          "verbatim": ""},
   "recommendation_strength": "not_stated",
   "evidence_quote": "", "evidence_locator": ""},
  {"finding_type": "outcome",
   "subject_drug": "...",
   "member_state": "",
   "outcome": {"measure": "", "result": "", "unit": "", "instrument": "",
               "is_requirement": false, "requirement_type": ""},
   "population_context": {...},
   "evidence_quote": "", "evidence_locator": ""}
]

Ivanovic, A. Palma, V. Pantò, L. Raﬀaelli English version: M.G. Toma PRESS AND COMMUNICATION OFFICE LAYOUT E GRAPHIC DESIGN EDITING: I. Comessatti C. D’Ambrosio, B. Galante, E. Iorio, F. Pomponi Please quote the Report as follows: Medicines on the Horizon. Report Year 2021. Rome: Italian Medicines Agency, 2021. ISBN 979­12­80335­09­8 The Report is available at the following website: www.aifa.gov.it Medicines on the Horizon 2021 3 Table of contents INTRODUCTION 4 SUMMARY 8 SECTION I MEDICINAL PRODUCTS AUTHORISED IN 2020 12 New medicinal products 14 Medicinal products containing new active substances 16 Biosimilars 28 Generics 32 New therapeutic indications of already authorised medicinal products 37 SECTION II MEDICINAL PRODUCTS AUTHORISED IN THE THREE-YEAR PERIOD 2018-2020 52 Medicinal products authorised in the three­year period 2018­2020 53 New medicinal products 53 New therapeutic indications of already authorised medicinal products 56 SECTION III MEDICINAL PRODUCTS UNDER EVALUATION IN 2021 57 New medicinal products 58 Medicinal products containing new active substances 60 Analysis of therapeutic indications 69 Biosimilars 72 Generics 74 SECTION IV PRIME MEDICINES 76 APPENDIX 88 ATC Legend 89 Glossary 90 Introduction The Medicines on the Horizon Report is intended to provide information on new medicinal products and most promising therapies, which received a positive opinion from the European Medicines Agency (EMA) in 2020 or which are expected to receive an opinion during the following years. The Report is part of the horizon scanning activities carried out by the Italian Medicines Agency (AIFA). These activities allow to identify and assess, at an earlier stage, new medicines and new therapeutic indications of already authorised medicinal products. This will allow to expand the number of treatment options available to physicians and patients and address unmet medical needs. In some cases, these therapies could have a significant impact on the national healthcare system (NHS) and would require AIFA to define suitable strategies for ensuring patients’ access to innovative and customised therapies. In the present analysis, medicines subject to a centralised approval procedure are considered, for which pharmaceutical companies submit a request for marketing authorisation (MA) to the European Medicines Agency. Such MA will then be valid in all EU Member States and in the European Economic Area (Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway). EMA’s Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use (CHMP) performs the scientific assessment of the application, and issues an opinion regarding the granting of the MA. EMA’s opinion is examined and validated by the European Commission1. The decision is then published in the Official Journal (OJ) of the European Union. Once the MA is granted, the medicinal product can be made available to all patients in the EU. Before the medicinal product is marketed in Italy, AIFA establishes the relevant supply regime, as well as price and reimbursement conditions, through its Technical-Scientific Committee (CTS) and Price and Reimbursement Committee (CPR). Specifically, within 60 days from the date in which the EC decision on the MA is published in the OJ, AIFA publishes a resolution in the Italian Official Journal concerning the placing of the medicinal product in question in a specific category named “Cnn class” (non-negotiated class C, that 1 http://ec.europa.eu/health/documents/community-register/html/index_en.htm Medicines on the Horizon 2021 5 Introduction TORNA ALL'INDICE is dedicated to medicines whose reimbursement conditions have not been evaluated yet), and defines its supply regime. This decision is published pending submission, by the pharmaceutical company, of an application for placing the product in a class for reimbursement and price negotiation purposes, which is necessary for having the medicinal product reimbursed by the NHS2. In order to market a medicinal product that is not reimbursed by the NHS, the MAH is required to give AIFA prior notice of its price and market launch date, in addition to complying with the conditions or restrictions regarding the safe and effective use of the medicinal product, where appropriate. The Medicines on the Horizon Report consists of four sections. The first section gives information on new medicines and new therapeutic indications of already authorised medicinal products that received a positive opinion by the CHMP in 2020. The second section provides an overview of new medicines and new therapeutic indications of already authorised medicinal products authorised during the three-year period 2018-2020. The third section concerns new medicines under evaluation that are expected to receive a CHMP opinion during 2021. Regarding authorised medicinal products, 50% are antineoplastic and immunomodulating agents for the treatment of certain solid tumours (e.g., lung cancer, breast cancer and ovarian cancer) and blood tumours (lymphoma, leukaemia, myeloma). A significant percentage concerns medicines for anti-infectives for systemic use (~20%) and, to a lesser extent, alimentary tract and metabolism, medicines for blood disorders. Among orphan medicines that received a positive EMA opinion, 3 are advanced therapy medicinal products (ATMPs), specifically gene therapies: Zolgensma (for the treatment of spinal muscular atrophy), Tecartus (for the treatment of mantle cell lymphoma) and Libmeldy (for the treatment of metachromatic leukodystrophy). bedrock_calls.system_prompt:
You are an HTA and Market Access strategist extracting structured evidence from one source document for a JCA (Joint Clinical Assessment) comparator and outcome scoping request.

You will be told the REQUESTED INTERVENTION and the REQUESTED POPULATION. Extract every distinct claim the document makes that is relevant to comparator or outcome scoping.

CRITICAL - DO NOT HALLUCINATE:
- Use ONLY information explicitly stated in the provided text. Never use outside medical knowledge to fill a gap, infer a typical dose, assume a standard comparator, or complete a partial fact with what is usually true.
- If a field is not explicitly stated, its value MUST be an empty string. Never invent a value to avoid leaving something blank.
- Do not paraphrase in a way that adds specificity the text did not have.

FIELD DEFINITIONS - read these; they are not self-evident:

subject_drug: the drug this specific claim is ABOUT - the treatment being assessed, studied or recommended in the passage you are extracting from. A document about a disease often discusses several drugs. If the passage is about a DIFFERENT drug than the requested intervention, say so here. Never write the requested intervention's name unless the passage is genuinely about it.

comparator.as_stated: the treatment this claim names as a comparison, alternative or standard of care - exactly as the source words it, including a regimen's full component list. A drug name, a named regimen, or a legitimate generic category the source states as the most specific thing available ("best supportive care", "physician's choice of chemotherapy"). NOT a sentence, NOT a trial name, NOT a statistical annotation.

comparator.role - choose exactly one:
  "active_comparator"  - studied, recommended or required AS the comparison for the subject drug in the population this passage describes
  "prior_therapy"      - treatment the patient RECEIVED BEFORE reaching this population (e.g. an induction regimen preceding a maintenance-phase question). This is treatment history, NOT a comparator
  "background_therapy" - given to all arms as a backbone, not the thing being compared
  "intervention_arm"   - this IS the subject drug's own arm, not a comparator
  "unclear"            - the passage does not let you tell
Getting this wrong is the single most common error: an induction-phase backbone named near the right population is prior therapy, not a comparator.

comparator.components: for a combination regimen, the complete list of substances AS ONE SOURCE STATES THEM. Never pool components from two different regimens that share an ingredient.

comparator.comparator_scenario - from the source's own language, choose one:
  "unique" (names one comparator) | "each_required" (several, required together) |
  "at_least_one" (several, at least one acceptable) | "individualised" (a bundle of options chosen by patient characteristics)

comparator.retain_all_status: "confirmed_droppable" or "confirmed_must_retain" ONLY when the source itself states a droppability preference. Otherwise "unconfirmed" - which will be the case for the great majority of sources, because this is a procedural preference, not a clinical fact. Never infer it.

DO NOT populate any drug class or mechanism for the comparator. That is resolved downstream from the comparator's own substance identity. If you write a class here it will be the SUBJECT drug's class, which is the exact error this instruction prevents.

population_context.*: the disease/population context THE SOURCE ITSELF states for this claim, in the source's own words - distinct from the requested population, which may be broader or narrower. Fill line_of_therapy, prior_therapy, stage, biomarker and treatment_setting_intent with what THIS passage says, never with the requested population's own label. If the passage states an interval since prior therapy or since relapse, put it in "other".

recommendation_strength (clinical guidelines only): "preferred" | "conditional_alternative" | "not_recommended" | "not_stated", as the guideline itself grades it. Never present a conditional or alternative recommendation as preferred.

outcome.measure: the outcome or endpoint named.
outcome.result: the reported figure, if any, exactly as stated.
outcome.unit: the unit of measurement EXACTLY as the source reports it (e.g. "months, median", "% of patients", "HR (95% CI)") - never invented, never assumed from general knowledge of what a typical unit would be.
outcome.instrument: the named instrument, where the source names one (e.g. a specific questionnaire). Empty otherwise.
outcome.is_requirement: true when the source states this outcome as one an assessment REQUIRES or EXPECTS in scope (an HTA methods document, an assessment scope table, a guideline's stated outcome set). false when the source is merely REPORTING a result for it. These are different things and the distinction matters more than the value.
outcome.requirement_type: "relative_effect_required" | "descriptive_only" | "" - only when the source states it.

evidence_quote: a VERBATIM span copied from the text that contains this claim. It must appear character-for-character in the text. If you cannot copy such a span, omit the whole record rather than paraphrasing.
evidence_locator: where in the document it sits (section heading, table number, page), if the text makes that visible.

member_state: the country whose body/guideline this claim belongs to, when the document is a national source. "EU-wide" for an EU-level record. Empty if unclear.

MULTIPLE POPULATIONS IN ONE DOCUMENT: a document can describe several populations for the same drug. Output SEPARATE records, one per population the text actually describes. Each comparator stays attached to the population it was ACTUALLY reported against - never pulled into the requested population's record just because the same document also discusses that population elsewhere.

Return ONLY a JSON array, no preamble, no markdown fences. Empty array if the document contains nothing relevant:
[

   "subject_drug": "...",
   "member_state": "",
   "comparator": {"as_stated": "", "role": "active_comparator", "is_combination": false,
                  "components": [], "comparator_scenario": "", "retain_all_status": "unconfirmed"},
   "population_context": {"disease": "", "subtype_histology": "", "stage": "", "biomarker": "",
                          "line_of_therapy": "", "prior_therapy": "",
                          "treatment_setting_intent": "", "age_band": "", "other": "",
                          "verbatim": ""},

  {"finding_type": "outcome",
   "subject_drug": "...",
   "member_state": "",

               "is_requirement": false, "requirement_type": ""},
   "population_context": {...},
   "evidence_quote": "", "evidence_locator": ""}

DOCUMENT TEXT:
Press release no. 4/2025 29/01/2025 AIFA Board of Directors approves the reimbursability of 13 medicines The Board of Directors of the Italian Medicines Agency, which met on 29 January for the first session of 2025, has re-admitted to reimbursement, in all Regions, the drug BAQSIMI (glucagon nasal spray), a treatment for severe hypoglycaemia in adult and paediatric patients with diabetes mellitus. Among the new therapies that will be reimbursed by the National Health Service, there is also an antitumor medicine for metastatic prostate cancer (PLUVICTO), a medicine for osteoporosis in post-menopausal women (ELADYNOS) and two medicines for the treatment of diabetes mellitus (MOUNJARO and AWIQLI). PLUVICTO (Lutetium (177lu) Vipivotide Tetraxetan) is a radiopharmaceutical indicated for the treatment of adult patients with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer, which is administered intravenously in hospital. It is a precision therapy that combines a radioisotope with a molecule capable of recognizing and binding to a receptor expressed on tumour cells. The medicine, now reimbursed by the NHS, represents a new therapeutic option for prostate cancer, one of the most widespread cancers in the world. ELADYNOS (abaloparatide) is a new medicine in injectable solution for subcutaneous use indicated for osteoporosis in postmenopausal women at increased risk of fracture. MOUNJARO (tirzepatide) is indicated for the treatment of type 2 diabetes mellitus and AWIQLI (insulin icodec) is a weekly human insulin analogue. The Board of Directors approved the admission to reimbursement by the NHS of 13 medicines, including orphan drugs for rare diseases (1), new medicines of chemical origin (3), generic medicines (2), extensions of therapeutic indications (6 medicine for 12 new therapeutic indications) and biosimilars (1). Furthermore, 16 price renegotiations were approved, the majority of which involved price reductions while small increases were decided on for medicines at risk of shortages. The therapeutic extensions of medicines already reimbursed by the NHS mainly fall into the area of oncological diseases and concern the medicines JEMPERLI (ostarlimab), KEYTRUDA (pembrolizumab), OPDIVO (nivolumab), TRODELVY (sacituzumab govitecan) e XALKORI (crizotinib). Among the generics, an anticoagulant and an antipsychotic indicated for the treatment of schizophrenia were admitted to reimbursement. A biosimilar indicated for plaque psoriasis and Crohn's disease has also been admitted to reimbursement. A summary table with the medicines authorised and admitted for reimbursement by the SSN is attached to the press release. New medicines and extension of indications Board of Directors 29 January 2025* TYPE OF NEGOTIATION ATTIVO ACTIVE INGREDIENT MEDICINE THERAPEUTIC INDICATIONS Orphan drugs for rare diseases Abaloparatide ELADYNOS First-choice treatment in secondary prevention in women with previous vertebral or femoral fractures and T-score spine or femur <-2.5 and > -5.0 (T-score <-2.0 and > -5.0 if over 65 years of age) + ≥ 2 mild or at least 1 moderate vertebral fracture or history of fracture of the forearm, humerus, sacrum, pelvis, hip, femur, or tibia in the last 5 years. New chemical entities Insulina icodec AWIQLI Treatment of diabetes mellitus in adults. Tirzepatide MOUNJARO Type 2 diabetes mellitus - Mounjaro is indicated for the treatment of adults with inadequately controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus as an adjunct to diet and exercise: · as monotherapy when the use of metformin is considered inappropriate due to intolerance or contraindications · in addition to other medicinal products for the treatment of diabetes Pluvicto, in combination with androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) with or without androgen receptor (AR) pathway inhibitor, is indicated for the treatment of adult patients with progressive, prostate specific membrane antigen (PSMA) positive metastatic castration resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC) who have been treated with AR pathway inhibitor and taxane-based chemotherapy. Treatment of deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism (PE) and prevention of recurrent DVT and PE in adults (see section 4.4 for haemodynamically unstable patients with PE). Lurasidone LURASIDONE TEVA Indications under negotiation (already reimbursed for the originator medicinal product): Lurasidone Teva is indicated for the treatment of schizophrenia in adults and adolescents aged 13 years and above. Extension of therapeutic indications Ferric carboxymaltose FERINJECT Extension of indication in children and adolescents aged 1 to 13 years. Dostarlimab JEMPERLI JEMPERLI is indicated in combination with carboplatin and paclitaxel for the treatment of adult patients with advanced or recurrent primary mismatch repair deficiency (dMMR)/microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H) endometrial cancer (EC) and who are candidates for systemic therapy. Pembrolizumab KEYTRUDA KEYTRUDA, in combination with trastuzumab, a fluoropyrimidine- and platinum-containing chemotherapy, is indicated for the first-line treatment of HER2-positive locally advanced unresectable or metastatic adenocarcinoma of the stomach or gastroesophageal junction in adults whose tumours express PD-L1 with a CPS ≥ 1. Pembrolizumab KEYTRUDA KEYTRUDA, in combination with fluoropyrimidine- and platinum-containing chemotherapy, is indicated for the first-line treatment of HER2-negative locally advanced unresectable or metastatic adenocarcinoma of the stomach or gastroesophageal junction in adults whose tumours express PD-L1 with a CPS ≥ 1. Pembrolizumab KEYTRUDA KEYTRUDA monotherapy is indicated for the adjuvant treatment of adults with renal cell carcinoma at increased risk of recurrence following nephrectomy or following nephrectomy and resection of metastatic lesions. Pembrolizumab KEYTRUDA KEYTRUDA, in combination with gemcitabine and cisplatin, is indicated for the first-line treatment of locally advanced unresectable or metastatic biliary tract cancer in adults. Pembrolizumab KEYTRUDA KEYTRUDA, in combination with platinum-containing chemotherapy as neoadjuvant treatment and then continued as monotherapy as adjuvant treatment, is indicated for the treatment of resectable non-small cell lung cancer at high risk of recurrence in adults. Nivolumab OPDIVO OPDIVO in combination with platinum-containing chemotherapy is indicated for the neoadjuvant treatment of resectable non-small cell lung cancer at high risk of recurrence in adult patients with tumour PD-L1 expression ≥ 1%. Nivolumab OPDIVO OPDIVO monotherapy is indicated for the adjuvant treatment of adults and adolescents aged 12 years and older with stage IIB or IIC melanoma or melanoma with lymph node involvement or metastatic disease who have undergone complete resection. Sacituzumab govitecan TRODELVY Trodelvy monotherapy is indicated for the treatment of adult patients with hormone receptor (HR)-positive, HER2-negative, metastatic or unresectable breast cancer who have received prior endocrine therapy and at least two other systemic therapies in the advanced setting. Crizotinib XALKORI The treatment of paediatric patients (= 6 to < 18 years) with unresectable, relapsed or refractory, anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK)-positive inflammatory myofibroblastic tumour (IMT) 2. Crizotinib XALKORI Treatment of paediatric patients (= 6 to < 18 years) with relapsed or refractory systemic type anaplastic large cell lymphoma (ALCL) positive for anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK). Biosimilar Ustekinumab OTULFI OTULFI 45 and 90 mg is indicated for the treatment of moderate to severe plaque psoriasis in adult patients who have failed to respond to, or who have a contraindication to, or who are intolerant to other systemic therapies, including ciclosporin, methotrexate (MTX), or PUVA (psoralen and ultraviolet A). Plaque psoriasis in paediatric patients is indicated for the treatment of moderate to severe plaque psoriasis in paediatric and adolescent patients aged 6 years and older who are inadequately controlled by, or are intolerant to, other systemic therapies or phototherapy. AIFA RECOMMENDATIONS ON DRUGS for the home management of COVID-19 Vers.10 — Updated 10/03/2023 SYMPTOMATIC DRUGS Symptomatic therapy Acetaminophen or NSAIDs may be used in case of fever or joint or muscle pain (unless there is clear contraindication to use). Other symptomatic drugs may be used on clinical judgment. DRUGS TO BE USED ONLY AT SPECIFIC STAGES OF THE DISEASE Antivirals Remdesivir — Veklury ® information for healthcare professionals https://www.aifa.gov.it/aggio rnamento-sui-farmaci- utilizzabili-per-il-trattamento- della-malattia-covid19 Nirmatrelvir/ritonavir — Paxlovid ® Information for healthcare professionals https://www.ema.europa.eu/ en/medicines/human/summa ries-opinion/paxlovid Two antivirals (remdesivir, nirmatrelvir/ritonavir) are currently authorised by EMA to treat adults with COVID-19 who do not require additional oxygen therapy and are at increased risk of progression to severe COVID-19 forms. The patient should not be hospitalised due to COVID-19, have a mild-to-moderate form and at least one of the following risk factors associated with the development of severe disease: • Oncological/oncohematological pathology in active phase • Chronic kidney failure • Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and/or other chronic respiratory disease (e.g. people with asthma, pulmonary fibrosis or who need oxygen therapy for reasons other than SARS-CoV-2) • Primary or acquired immunodeficiency • Obesity (BMI >30) • Cardio-cerebrovascular disease (heart failure, coronary heart disease, cardiomyopathy, hypertension with concomitant organ damage, stroke) • Uncompensated diabetes mellitus (HbA1c> 9.0 % 75 mmol/mol) or with chronic complications • Age>65 years • Chronic Hepatopathy • Hemoglobinopathies • Neurodevelopmental disorders and neurodegenerative diseases Remdesivir is an antiviral drug (nucleotide analogue prodrug of adenosine), already authorised by EMA for the treatment of COVID-19 with pneumonia requiring additional oxygen therapy, which obtained in December 2021 authorisation for the extension of the indication related to the treatment of COVID-19 for people ‘who do not require additional oxygen therapy and have an increased risk of progression to severe COVID-19”. Treatment should be initiated as soon as possible after the diagnosis of COVID-19 and within 7 days of the onset of symptoms. The recommended dosage of remdesivir in adults is: • day 1: single loading dose of remdesivir 200 mg administered by intravenous infusion • from day 2 onwards: 100 mg given once daily as an intravenous infusion. The total duration of treatment should be 3 days. Patients should be monitored during treatment with remdesivir. Administration of the drug in an outpatient setting should be monitored according to local practice. Use should take place under conditions where severe hypersensitivity reactions, including anaphylaxis, can be treated. For the prescribing and monitoring of outcomes, an AIFA web log will be compiled. Paxlovid® (nirmatrelvir-ritonavir) is the first oral antiviral drug to have been authorised by EMA for the treatment of COVID-19 in adults, not hospitalised and at high risk of developing a serious COVID-19 disease. The medicinal product contains two active substances, nirmatrelvir and ritonavir, present in two separate tablets: nirmatrelvir works by reducing the ability of SARS-CoV-2 to replicate in the body, while ritonavir (a drug that has long been used in the treatment of HIV infection) has no antiviral activity but works as a pharmacological booster by prolonging the action of nirmatrelvir. Paxlovid® should be administered as soon as possible after the diagnosis of COVID-19, no later than 5 days after the onset of symptoms. Treatment consists of taking two nirmatrelvir tablets and one ritonavir tablet twice daily for 5 days. For warnings and precautions of use see Summary of Product Characteristics — SmPC (https:// www.ema.europa.eu/en/documents/product-information /paxlovid-epar-product-information_en.pdf). Prescribers need to accurately investigate the patient’s pharmacological history as ritonavir has important drug interactions with many drugs, in relation to which warnings and recommendations have been included in Paxlovid product information. For further support in the evaluation of possible drug interactions, it is recommended to consult the website: https://www.covid19-druginteractions.org/ . For Paxlovid there is a two-fold way of prescribing: - by the COVID centre specialist through AIFA web register and direct distribution by Health Companies identified by the Regions - by GPs through a dematerialised prescription and compilation of the AIFA web Therapeutic Plan and dispensing through proximity pharmacies through distribution “on behalf”. Monoclonal antibodies casirivimab/imdevimab — Ronapreve® (600/600 mg) information for healthcare professionals https://www.aifa.gov.it/uso- degli-anticorpi-monoclonali sotrovimab — Xevudy ® information for healthcare professionals https://www.aifa.gov.it/uso- degli-anticorpi-monoclonali tixagevimab/cilgavimab — Evushled® information for healthcare professionals https://www.aifa.gov.it/uso- degli-anticorpi-monoclonali The monoclonal antibodies available in Italy, authorised by EMA for the treatment of SARS-CoV-2 infection in people at high risk of progression to severe disease, are as follows: the casirivimab/imdevimab combination, sotrovimab, and the tixagevimab/cilgavimab combination. In the early stages of the outbreak, the bamlanivimab/etesevimab combination was made available, pursuant to Article 5.2 of Legislative Decree 219/2006 (Ministerial Decree of 6 February 2021 and 12 July 2021); its authorisation for emergency distribution ceased on 31 July 2022. The population eligible for treatment with the three treatments is as follows: people aged 12 years and older (and at least 40 kg), positive for SARS-CoV-2, non-hospitalised for COVID-19, not on COVID-19 oxygen therapy, with mild-to-moderate symptoms and who are at high risk of severe COVID-19. Possible risk factors include the following: • age > 65 years; • a Body Mass Index (BMI) ≥ 30, or > 95% percentile by age and gender; • chronic kidney failure, including peritoneal dialysis or haemodialysis; • uncontrolled diabetes mellitus (HbA1c ≥ 9.0 % or 75 mmol/mol) or with chronic complications; • primary or secondary immunodeficiency; • cardio-cerebrovascular disease (including hypertension with concomitant organ damage) • chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and/or other chronic respiratory disease (e.g. people with asthma, pulmonary fibrosis or who need oxygen therapy for reasons other than SARS-CoV-2); • Chronic Hepatopathy • Hemoglobinopathies • Neurodevelopmental disorders and neurodegenerative diseases. COVID-19 must be recently onset (however for no later than 7 days). Treatment is possible more than seven days after onset only in subjects with immunodeficiency who have: negative serology for SARS-CoV-2 and prolonged positivity to the molecular buffer. For all types of treatment, a single administration is provided at the following dosages: - casirivimab (600 mg) + imdevimab (600 mg) IV;the combination may be administered at the same subcutaneous dose if intravenous administration is not feasible and results in a delay in treatment. - sotrovimab (500 mg) IV - tixagevimab (300 mg)/cilgavimab (300 mg) IM, with two separate and sequential injections. For modalities and duration see information for healthcare professionals (https://www.aifa.gov.it/uso-degli-anticorpi-monoclonali). Administration should be monitored for up to one hour after the end of the infusion by a properly trained healthcare professional and able to handle any serious adverse reactions. For the prescription and monitoring of 30-day outcomes, an AIFA web log will be compiled. The effectiveness of monoclonal antibodies may be reduced against certain viral variants;this should also be taken into account in the therapeutic choice in relation to the local epidemiological situation, for which reference is made to the flash surveys periodically published by the ISS. Although no published clinical studies are available, there is evidence from in vitro studies assessing the neutralising efficacy of different monoclonal antibodies. For an up-to-date overview of in vitro efficacy against different variants it is recommended to consult Stanford University’s website (Stanford University’s Coronavirus Antiviral & Resistance Databasand; https://covdb.stanford.edu/susceptibility- data/table-mab-susc/ ), updated in real time and used as a reference also by the main international bodies. When interpreting these data, it should be considered that other intrinsic characteristics (such as those related to the effectiveness of different antibodies) could have an impact on clinical efficacy compared to the currently prevailing variants. In general, based on the advancement of knowledge, diagnostic availability, possible logistical and organisational difficulties and the epidemiological situation, it may be considered the opportunity to determine the viral variant involved in the infection before deciding on which antibody or combination of monoclonal antibodies to guide the therapeutic choice. It should be noted that these data are constantly evolving and that therefore the indication to the use of specific monoclonal antibodies may vary over time depending on the variant of SARS-CoV-2 prevailing in the country and its sensitivity to the different products available. The study that showed reduced mortality with low doses of corticosteroids used dexamethasone at a dosage of 6 mg for up to 10 days. Any other corticosteroids should be used at equivalent dosages (methylprednisolone 32 mg, prednisone 40 mg, hydrocortisone 160 mg). Finally, it is important to remember that in many people with chronic diseases the use of cortisone can lead to important adverse events that risk complicating the course of the viral disease. As an example known to all, that of diabetic subjects in which both the presence of an infection and the use of cortisone can severely destabilise glycemic control. Heparins AIFA Information sheet: https://www.aifa.gov.it/aggio rnamento-sui-farmaci- utilizzabili-per-il-trattamento- della-malattia-covid19 The use of heparins (usually low molecular weight heparins) in prophylaxis of thromboembolic events in the medical patient with acute respiratory infection and reduced mobility is recommended by the main guidelines and should continue throughout the period of immobility. Routine use of heparins is not recommended in non-hospitalised and unassailed individuals due to the infectious episode, as there is no evidence of a clinical benefit in this patient/disease setting. Prophylactic dosages of the various heparinic compounds available may be used in the case of an allotted subject. It is important to remember that SARS-CoV-2 infection is not a contraindication to continue oral anticoagulant therapy (with AVK or NAO) or antiaggregating even double therapy already underway. MEDICINES NOT RECOMMENDED FOR THE TREATMENT OF COVID-19 Molnupiravir — Lagevrio ® Molnupiravir, an antiviral drug (prodrug metabolised to ribonucleosidic analogue N-hydroxycitidine), was initially made available through emergency distribution authorisation pursuant to Art.5.2 of DL 219/2006 (Ministerial Decree of 26 November 2021 and subsequent extensions). Following the negative opinion issued by the CHMP for the failure to demonstrate a clinical benefit in terms of reduced mortality and hospitalisations, the Agency suspended the use of the drug on 10/03/2023. Antibiotics AIFA Information Sheet (relative to azithromycin): https://www.aifa.gov.it/aggio rnamento-sui-farmaci- utilizzabili-per-il-trattamento- of the-disease-covid19 The use of antibiotics is not recommended for the treatment of SARS-CoV-2 infection. Recent well-conducted randomised clinical trials (which in most cases assessed the effectiveness of azithromycin) have shown that the use of an antibiotic, alone or associated with other drugs, with particular reference to hydroxychloroquine, does not alter the clinical course of the disease. The use of an antibiotic can only be considered when the presence of a bacterial overlap is suspected, in relation to the general clinical picture of the patient. Unjustified use of antibiotics can also result in the onset and spread of bacterial resistance that could impair the response to future antibiotic therapies. Hydroxychloroquine AIFA Information sheet: https://www.aifa.gov.it/aggio rnamento-sui-farmaci- utilizzabili-per-il-trattamento- of the-disease-covid19 The use of chloroquine or hydroxychloroquine is not recommended for the purpose of preventing or treating infection. The randomised clinical trials published to date conclude that the drug is substantially ineffective in the face of an increase in adverse events, albeit not serious. This makes the relationship between the benefits and risks of using this drug negative. Lopinavir/ritonavir Darunavir/ritonavir or cobicistat AIFA Information sheet :https://www.aifa.gov.it/aggi o rnamento-sui-farmaci- utilizzabili-per-il-trattamento- of the-disease-covid19 The use of lopinavir/ritonavir or darunavir/ritonavir or cobicistat is not recommended for the purpose of preventing or treating infection. The randomised clinical trials published to date all conclude for the ineffectiveness of these pharmacological approaches. The recommendations provided reflect the existing literature and guidance and will be updated in relation to the rapid evolution of scientific evidence. For more details on the individual data sheets, you can consult the AIFA institutional website at the following link:: https://www.aifa.gov.it/aggiornamento- sui-farmaci-utilizzabili-per-il-trattamento-della-malattia-covid19 . Oxygen therapy, which is an essential therapeutic presence in the presence of respiratory failure and for which proper use refers to the specific recommendations, is excluded from the guidelines provided. In addition to these recommendations, it should be noted that people on chronic treatment (e.g. with antihypertensives, ACE inhibitors or statins) are recommended to continue their treatment until different provisions of their doctor. People undergoing chronic immunosuppressive treatment due to a previous solid organ transplant rather than diseases with immune-mediated pathogenesis may continue the ongoing pharmacological treatment unless otherwise indicated by the treating specialist.

# Munkaköri/szakmai orvosi alkalmasság megítéléséhez szükséges ismeretek a megterhelésről és a munkakörülményekről

A munkaköri/szakmai orvosi alkalmasság megítéléséhez szükséges ismeretek a megterhelésről és a munkakörülményekről

Munkavégzés közben az emberi szervezetre ható megterhelés több tényezőből tevődik össze: a munkakörnyezet, munkaeszközök, maga a munkavégzés (energiafelhasználás, igénybevétel), azaz a baleseti és egészségkárosító kockázatok, körülmények, kóroki tényezők.

Munkaköri alkalmasság, illetve szakmai alkalmasság esetében az adott szakma/munkakör baleseti és egészségkárosító kockázatait, körülményeit, kóroki tényezőit a vizsgáló orvosnak ismernie kell.

Szakmai orvosi alkalmassági vizsgálat véleményezésekor az adott szakma követelményeit vesszük figyelembe, a gyakorlatok során milyen feladatokat kell elsajátítania a tanulónak (pl. hegesztés, programozás), milyen munkaeszközökkel kell dolgoznia (pl. lőfegyver), ezek alapján tudjuk felmérni a kóroki tényezőket, körülményeket. Az aktuális képzési és kimeneti követelmények, illetve a programtanterveket az adott ágazathoz tartozó, adott szakmáról itt található meg: <https://akkreditaltvizsgaztatas.ikk.hu/kkk-ptt>

Munkaköri orvosi alkalmassági vizsgálat esetében az adott munkahely, munkakör pontos ismerete (munkahigiénés bejárás, kockázatértékelés alapján) szükséges, hogy minden ***kóroki tényezőt, körülményt figyelembe vegyünk.***

# Munkaköri/szakmai orvosi alkalmasság megítéléséhez szükséges ismeretek a megterhelésről és a munkakörülményekről

A munkaköri/szakmai orvosi alkalmasság megítéléséhez szükséges ismeretek a megterhelésről és a munkakörülményekről

Munkavégzés közben az emberi szervezetre ható megterhelés több tényezőből tevődik össze: a munkakörnyezet, munkaeszközök, maga a munkavégzés (energiafelhasználás, igénybevétel), azaz a baleseti és egészségkárosító kockázatok, körülmények, kóroki tényezők.

Munkaköri alkalmasság, illetve szakmai alkalmasság esetében az adott szakma/munkakör baleseti és egészségkárosító kockázatait, körülményeit, kóroki tényezőit a vizsgáló orvosnak ismernie kell.

Szakmai orvosi alkalmassági vizsgálat véleményezésekor az adott szakma követelményeit vesszük figyelembe, a gyakorlatok során milyen feladatokat kell elsajátítania a tanulónak (pl. hegesztés, programozás), milyen munkaeszközökkel kell dolgoznia (pl. lőfegyver), ezek alapján tudjuk felmérni a kóroki tényezőket, körülményeket. Az aktuális képzési és kimeneti követelmények, illetve a programtanterveket az adott ágazathoz tartozó, adott szakmáról itt található meg: <https://akkreditaltvizsgaztatas.ikk.hu/kkk-ptt>

Observational No  160 36 Call AIFA 2017 – Study protocol ϳ Synopsis (max 4.000 characters) This sections should include: Background, Objectives, Methods, Expected results Background: The recent introduction of new drugs targeting immune-checkpoints such as CTLA4, PD-1 and PD-L1 has revolutionized the treatment of several solid neoplasms including advanced melanoma and non small cell lung cancer. They act through an indirect stimulation of the immune system against neoplastic cells by inducing consistent and, often, durable anti-tumor responses. These treatments exert profound effects on immune cells within the tumor microenvironment mainly by recruiting tumor-infiltrating leukocytes and modifying the production of inflammatory and immune-related factors, which may spread into the circulation becoming possible disease markers. Immune-checkpoint inhibitors seem to be more effective in female patients, probably due to the influence of sex hormones on the immune response. Estrogens exert their function on the immune response also by a G protein-coupled estrogen receptor (GPER), activating signaling pathways distinct from that of ERa and ERb. In pre-clinical studies on melanoma, GPER signaling promotes a reduction in PD-L1 expression and inhibits tumor cell proliferation. GPER is involved in inflammatory processes regulation induced by cytokines. Interestingly, GPER overexpression has been also identified in NSCLC, suggesting a putative modulation of immune response by sex hormones also in NSCLC. Objectives: The present study aims to investigate in a real-world population whether inflammatory or immune-related biomarkers can be used as gender-specific predictive markers of response, toxicity and resistance to immune-checkpoint inhibitors in advanced melanoma and NSCLC. Methods: This will be an observational, prospective, multicenter, real-world study, conducted over a 3-year period in 160 patients (80 metastatic melanoma and 80 metastatic NSCLC), according to GCP, ethical norms and Italian laws regulating personal privacy. Patients will be consecutively enrolled in 5 clinical Units in the first year, treated with anti-PD1 (nivolumab or pembrolizumab) or anti-CTLA4 (ipilimumab) following criteria established by AIFA and followed up successively for 2 years. Blood samples will be collected at the same time points of blood withdrawal for the safety monitoring (about 15 time points in a 2-year period; at baseline, at each drug administration for the first six doses; successively at each instrumental tumor evaluation, and at the eventual confirmation of progression). Inflammatory and immune-related markers (MCP-1; IP-10; G-CSF; GM-CSF; IFNalpha; IFN-gamma; IL-1alpha; IL-1beta; IL-2; IL-4; IL-5; IL-6; IL-8; IL-10; IL-13; IL-17A; TGFbeta; TNFalpha; VEGF; angiopoietin; PCR and sPD-L1) will be measured in serum or plasma in a centralized reference laboratory using immunometric methods (including Luminex xMAP technology). Analysis of correlation networks will be performed. As primary endpoint, the association between marker changes and the response to treatment divided according to gender will be assessed. Secondary endpoints will be the study of marker correlation with PFS, OS and tolerability. A trial clinical unit will prepare e-CRF, monitor all phases of the study and perform the statistical analysis. Expected results: The identification of new predictive biomarkers, beside allowing for the early identification of responses to treatment avoiding early suspension of therapy or its potentially harmful extension, will provide a background for gender-tailored treatments. This proposal aims at impacting on the optimization of immune-checkpoint inhibitors administration in relation to real progressive disease and gender response prediction, thus contributing to improve the economical sustainability of these treatments within the Italian National Health System.
