To make the plan, they’ll assess where the cancer has grown. Your team may also test the cancer cells for unique markers.
After diagnosing non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), your care team will focus on treating the cancer. Tests are needed to learn more about the cancer and your overall health.
Planning treatment with a team evaluation It takes a team to plan treatment of NSCLC. If more than one type of treatment is an option, your team will consist of members from different fields of medicine, such as: h A thoracic surgical oncologist, an expert in removing cancer from the chest h A medical oncologist, an expert in treating cancer with drugs h A radiation oncologist, an expert in treating cancer with radiation Many people also have team members who provide supportive care, which is discussed in Chapter 4: Improving life with supportive care.
You are an important part of the team. Your participation is as important as that of any specialist on your team.
First tests for cancer staging Your team needs to assess the extent of the lung cancer in your body. This is called staging the cancer. They also need to assess your overall health.
There are 4 main stages of lung cancer. You may see them written with Roman numerals— stages I (1), II (2), III (3), and IV (4). Higher stages mean a greater extent of cancer.
The first tests used for cancer staging and to assess your overall health are described in this section and listed in Guide 3.
Medical history Expect your team to ask a lot of questions about your health. This is known as taking a medical history.
Guide 3 First tests for early and locally advanced non-small cell lung cancers • Medical history including weight loss • Physical exam • Performance status • Complete blood count • Chemistry profile • CT scan with contrast of the chest and upper abdomen 21 NCCN Guidelines for Patients® Early & Locally Advanced Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer 3 Testing for early and locally advanced NSCLC Your team will want to know about your past and current health, such as: h Illnesses and injuries h Symptoms like unexplained weight loss, trouble breathing, chest pain, and cough h Prescribed and over-the-counter medicines and supplements h Previous surgeries h Lifestyle choices, including your diet, how active you are, and whether you smoke or drink alcohol Also be prepared to discuss the health of your close blood relatives. Such family members include siblings, parents, and grandparents related to you by birth.
Physical exam A team member will also perform a thorough physical exam of your body. This exam may include: h Checking your vital signs—blood pressure, heart rate, breathing rate, and body temperature h Feeling or listening to organs, including your lungs, spleen, and liver h Feeling for enlarged lymph nodes, which are small disease-fighting structures throughout your body h Assessing your level of pain, if any, when you are touched Performance status Performance status is your ability to do day-to-day activities. It's based on your medical history and exam. Your team will use your Physical exam Your care team will gain important information from a physical exam of your body. The exam may reveal areas of cancer growth.
22 NCCN Guidelines for Patients® Early & Locally Advanced Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer 3 Testing for early and locally advanced NSCLC performance status to decide if your body can endure intense treatment.
Blood tests Blood tests are commonly used to screen for disease. They are also used to assess if cancer is affecting organs. Samples of your blood will be needed for these blood tests: h A complete blood count measures parts of the blood, including counts of white blood cells, red blood cells, and platelets. h A chemistry profile assesses sugar and natural salts in your body and how well your liver and kidneys are working.
CT scan A CT (computed tomography) scan is often the first scan done to stage lung cancer. If you had a CT scan more than 60 days ago, you should have the scan again so your team has current information.
A CT scan is a more detailed kind of x-ray. It takes many pictures from different angles. A computer combines the images to make 3D pictures.
You'll receive an injection of contrast if it's safe for you. Contrast is a substance that makes images clearer.
Your team will look for tumors in images of your chest and upper abdomen, including the adrenal glands.
Additional scans for cancer staging Using the first set of tests, your team will start deciding what the stage of the cancer is. You’ll likely have more tests to confirm the stage and your treatment options. A list of possible additional tests is in Guide 4.
Besides a CT scan, you may have one or more of the scans described next to further assess where the lung cancer may have spread.
FDG-PET/CT scan A PET (positron emission tomography) scan combined with a CT scan is necessary for treatment planning. If you had a PET/CT scan more than 60 days ago, you should have the scan again so your team has current information.
Either your whole body will be scanned or the scan will extend from your neck to the middle of your thighs. Before the scan, you will be injected with a radiotracer called fluorodeoxyglucose, or FDG. The tracer makes even small amounts of cancer cells show up as hot (or bright) spots on the scan.
Multiple health problems can cause hot spots, so hot spots that suggest cancer often need to be confirmed by other tests.
Brain MRI Lung cancer tends to spread to the brain. Most people with lung cancer need a brain scan, but a brain scan isn't always needed for early cancers.
An MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) scan may show small brain tumors that aren’t 23 NCCN Guidelines for Patients® Early & Locally Advanced Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer 3 Testing for early and locally advanced NSCLC causing symptoms. MRI uses a safe magnetic field and radio waves to make images. Contrast will also be used unless it’s not safe for you. If you can’t have an MRI, you may get a CT scan of your head with contrast.
MRI of spine and thoracic inlet Superior sulcus tumors are lung cancers that start at the top of the lung. They typically grow into the chest wall and may grow next to your spine, blood vessels, or nerves. If these tumors have grown through the chest wall, MRI of your spine and thoracic inlet is needed. The thoracic inlet is the center of a ring of bones at the top of the ribcage.
Assessing the health of your lungs Imaging is one tool for assessing the health of your lungs. You may also need to have the procedures described in this section.
Bronchoscopy Bronchoscopy is a procedure that allows your team to see inside of your airways. Your team will evaluate the lung tumor seen on scans, look for other lung tumors, and assess for other health issues.
Bronchoscopy is done with a medical device called a bronchoscope. A bronchoscope has a small, flexible tube that is gently guided down your throat and into your airways.
A bronchoscopy is needed if: h You haven’t already had a bronchoscopy for diagnosis or cancer staging, and h The lung cancer will be treated with surgery.

A chest x-ray followed by CT started my journey of diagnosis and eventual treatment of early-stage lung cancer." “ 24 NCCN Guidelines for Patients® Early & Locally Advanced Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer 3 Testing for early and locally advanced NSCLC Bronchoscopy is often done on the day of surgery to save time and reduce costs and risks. Sometimes, bronchoscopy is done before surgery for a tumor in the middle of a lung.
Pulmonary function tests Pulmonary function tests are breathing activities used to assess how well your lungs work. Your team will use the results to decide if certain treatments are safe.
Testing lymph nodes for cancer When lung cancer spreads, it typically spreads to lymph nodes in the lung and then to lymph nodes outside of the lung.
Your care team will use imaging to decide which, if any, lymph nodes to sample for cancer testing. Lymph nodes may not need testing if the lung tumor is very small and on the side of your body away from the center.
Removed tissue will be sent to the lab for testing. Test results will be used to stage the cancer.
Mediastinal lymph nodes The space between your lungs, called the mediastinum, has many lymph nodes. Lung cancer is more likely to spread to these nodes when the tumor is larger and closer to this area.
Mediastinal lymph nodes can be reached by one of several procedures: h Mediastinoscopy involves a medical device that is inserted through a small cut in the neck.
Lymph node testing Lymph nodes are small structures throughout the body that help fight disease. It's very important for your care team to know which, if any, lymph nodes have cancer. There are a few methods for removing lymph nodes in and outside of the lungs. Bronchoscopy is one of those methods.
25 NCCN Guidelines for Patients® Early & Locally Advanced Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer 3 Testing for early and locally advanced NSCLC h Mediastinotomy is an open surgery of the middle of the chest done through a small cut near the breastbone. h Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS)-guided biopsy involves a medical device that is guided down your body's food tube (esophagus). h Endobronchial ultrasound (EBUS)-guided biopsy is performed using a bronchoscope.
EBUS- and EUS-guided lymph node biopsies are often done days ahead of surgical treatment.
Other lymph nodes Some lung cancers have spread to lymph nodes in the other lung or near the collarbone. Methods to biopsy these nodes include: h Excisional biopsy, which removes an entire node through a cut into the skin. h Thoracoscopy, a surgery that makes small openings into your chest through which small tools are inserted to see and remove tissue (also called video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery, or VATS). h An external needle biopsy, which involves guiding a thin needle through your skin and into a node.
Profiling cancer with biomarker tests Biomarker tests look for biological clues, or markers, that are used to make decisions about cancer care. Biomarkers differ between types of cancer and among people with the same type of cancer.
Biomarker testing may be done if NSCLC will be treated with prescribed drugs. Your medical oncologist will select treatment based on which biomarkers the cancer has.
Biomarker tests are performed on tumor tissue removed during a biopsy or surgery. A blood sample also may be tested. The cancer will be tested for several biomarkers, including: h Level of PD-L1, a protein on the surface of lung cancer cells h EGFR exon 19 deletion, a missing part of the EGFR gene h EGFR L858R mutation, a change in the EGFR gene h ALK gene fusion, a hybrid gene made from a part of the ALK gene and a part of another gene 26 NCCN Guidelines for Patients® Early & Locally Advanced Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer 3 Testing for early and locally advanced NSCLC Key points h Your care team will work together to plan treatment specific to you. h A member of your team will ask about your health, examine your body, and test blood samples. h Imaging can help show where the lung cancer may have grown and spread. h Your lungs may be examined by bronchoscopy, and your ability to breathe may be tested with pulmonary function tests. h To help stage the cancer, samples of lymph nodes inside or outside of the lungs may be removed and tested for cancer. h Biomarker tests look for small yet important features of cancer that differ between people. There are treatments for some biomarkers.
Questions to ask h Could the tests be wrong or cause health problems? h Will I need to pay for any of the tests? h What do I need to do to prepare for testing? h What are the procedures for removing and storing tissue samples for future testing? h How can I get a copy of the test results in case I want a second opinion?
What’s next? Your team will explain the test results to you and what they recommend for your cancer care. A care plan usually includes treatment for cancer and support for you. NCCN experts recommend starting supportive care early. You’ll find more information in Chapter 4: Improving life with supportive care. To learn what NCCN experts recommend for the main treatment of lung cancer, read Chapter 5: Planning primary treatment.

28 Starting supportive care early 28 Help to quit smoking 29 Managing common cancer effects 30 Addressing social and financial needs 30 Key points 31 Questions to ask 28 NCCN Guidelines for Patients® Early & Locally Advanced Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer 4 Improving life with supportive care Supportive care aims to improve your quality of life. A key part of care is reducing symptoms caused by cancer or treatment. Supportive care also provides help for social and financial needs.
The main concern for most people with cancer is to get treatment that works. But having cancer often involves additional challenges to one’s health and life. This chapter discusses what help is available for these challenges.
What is supportive care?
Supportive care is an important part of cancer care. The goal is to improve your quality of life during and after cancer treatment. Supportive care is for everyone with cancer and their families, not just for those at the end of life. It’s also known as palliative care.
Supportive care includes a wide range of services. Supportive care prevents or manages the symptoms of cancer and the side effects of cancer treatment, like pain and cancer-related fatigue. It also addresses the mental, social, emotional, and spiritual concerns faced by people with cancer.
Supportive care provides help with additional needs, such as: h Making treatment decisions h Coordinating your care h Paying for care h Planning for advance care and end of life Starting supportive care early NCCN experts recommend combining supportive care with treatment shortly after diagnosis of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Receiving supportive care early can be more helpful than starting supportive care later.
Specialists who may provide supportive care to you include a: h Palliative care specialist h Respiratory therapist h Rehabilitation specialist h Registered dietitian h Social worker Help to quit smoking Smoking can limit how well cancer treatment works. h If you don’t smoke, it’s important that you don’t start now. h If you do smoke, it's important to quit. It’s never too late.
Nicotine addiction is one of the hardest addictions to stop. The stress of having cancer may make it even harder to quit.
The library of NCCN Guidelines for Patients has several guides that focus on supportive care. The NCCN Guidelines for Patients: Quitting Smoking provides critical support and guidance for people with cancer. This guide explains how best to use the tools that exist to help you quit for good.
29 NCCN Guidelines for Patients® Early & Locally Advanced Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer 4 Improving life with supportive care If you tried to quit before, try again. Most people slip or relapse before quitting for good.
Managing common cancer effects NCCN has guides that address physical and emotional symptoms that are commonly caused by cancer or cancer treatment. They are briefly described next so you can find the information you need.
Palliative care The NCCN Guidelines for Patients: Palliative Care describes care for physical and emotional symptoms, such as: h Diarrhea, constipation, sleep issues h Stress and grief It also provides guidance on talking with your team about cancer treatment.
Distress Everyone with cancer feels distressed at some point. It's normal to feel worried, sad, helpless, or angry. NCCN Guidelines for Patients: Distress During Cancer Care empowers people to get help for distress.
Fatigue Cancer-related fatigue is not the typical tiredness that follows an active or long day. It’s a lack of energy that is distressing, does not improve with normal rest or sleep, and disrupts life. NCCN Guidelines for Patients: Fatigue and Cancer explains the ways to reduce cancer-related fatigue.
Nausea and vomiting Chemotherapy and radiation therapy are common cancer treatments that may cause nausea and vomiting. Nausea is the feeling that you are going to throw up. Vomiting is forcefully throwing up what’s in your stomach. Treatments that prevent and manage both conditions are discussed in NCCN Guidelines for Patients: Nausea and Vomiting. Supportive care resources The library of NCCN Guidelines for Patients has a series of guides on supportive care, available at NCCN.org/patientguidelines and on the NCCN Patient Guides for Cancer app.
30 NCCN Guidelines for Patients® Early & Locally Advanced Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer 4 Improving life with supportive care Low blood counts Chemotherapy often causes a drop in blood cells. Depending on the type of blood cell affected, you may have fatigue, unusual bleeding, and more infections than usual. Recommendations on how to manage low counts are described in NCCN Guidelines for Patients: Low Blood Counts.
Immunotherapy side effects Immune checkpoint inhibitors are used to treat many types of NSCLC. However, this treatment may cause your immune cells to attack your healthy cells. NCCN Guidelines for Patients: Immunotherapy Side Effects: Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors explains treatment for many types of side effects.
Blood clots Some drug treatments for NSCLC increase the risk for blood clots. A thrombus is a type of blood clot that can dangerously block blood flow. NCCN Guidelines for Patients: Blood Clots and Cancer explains ways to prevent and treat thrombi.
Addressing social and financial needs Many factors impact health outcomes. Your genes and the health care you receive are examples of important medical factors. But social factors are just as important. Social factors include: h Transportation h Housing and utility assistance h Access to food h Finances and work h Health insurance h Social support and safety NCCN experts recommend that your team monitors the impact of social factors on your health. Your team will make referrals to other professionals as needed.
Key points h Supportive care aims to improve your quality of life, including preventing and relieving symptoms. h Starting supportive care early has more benefits than starting later. h Quitting smoking may improve treatment results. h Getting help for social and financial needs may improve your well-being and health.
There's no concern that is too trivial or stupid for your oncologist to answer. They may incorrectly think I'm getting hospice care. h Who should I contact if my symptoms get worse?
What’s next? Additional information on receiving support is in Chapter 9: Lifelong survivorship care. Survivorship care is related to supportive care but focuses more on the long-term and late effects of cancer. Although survivorship care often begins after initial treatment ends, many care recommendations can be started during treatment to prevent or lessen cancer-related effects. If you’re looking for information on cancer treatment, a good place to start is Chapter 5: Planning primary treatment.
32 NCCN Guidelines for Patients® Early & Locally Advanced Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer 5 Planning primary treatment 33 Types of primary treatment 34 Staging lung cancer 36 Lung cancer stages 36 Treatment by clinical stage 38 Participating in a clinical trial 40 Key points 40 Questions to ask 33 NCCN Guidelines for Patients® Early & Locally Advanced Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer 5 Planning primary treatment Primary treatment is the main treatment used to rid your body of lung cancer. The options for primary treatment depend heavily on the cancer stage.
Surgery is a common treatment for early and locally advanced non-small cell lung cancers (NSCLCs), but it’s often not the only option. Read on to learn what your options for primary treatment may be.
Types of primary treatment Many people with NSCLC have multiple cancer treatments. The treatment that is most important is called primary treatment.
The type of primary treatment differs among people with early or locally advanced NSCLC. Primary treatment may be: h Surgery to remove tumors or body tissue with cancer h Radiation therapy, which most often uses high-energy x-rays to treat lung cancer h Chemoradiation, a combined treatment of prescribed drugs and radiation therapy Your care team will recommend a primary treatment for you. Which primary treatment you receive will depend largely on the cancer stage. A cancer stage is a rating of the growth and spread of cancer.
"When you are deciding your treatment, remember that even though some decisions need to be made fast, don't rush. Think through your options and get second, or even third, opinions. Have people you can trust to talk through your options so you feel comfortable in your decisions." 34 NCCN Guidelines for Patients® Early & Locally Advanced Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer 5 Planning primary treatment Staging lung cancer Lung cancer is staged using the tumor, node, metastasis (TNM) system maintained by the American Joint Committee on Cancer. Each letter in the system represents an area of cancer growth and is assigned a score.
T = Tumor score The T score describes the primary tumor. The primary tumor is the main group of cancer cells in the lung.
The T scores are based on: h The biggest width of the primary tumor measured in centimeters (cm) h Invasive growth of the primary tumor into nearby body parts, such as the chest wall h The number of tumors in a lung The T scores used in this guide are T1, T2a, T2b, T3, and T4. Higher numbers represent more growth. A brief description of the T scores is in Guide 5.
Guide 5 T (tumor) scores used to stage lung cancer T1 A T1 tumor is 3 cm or smaller. It’s no larger than a grape.
T2a A T2a tumor has one of these features: • Tumor is wider than 3 cm but no larger than 4 cm • Invasive growth into the next lobe, inner lining of the lung, or main airway • The tumor caused the lung to collapse or swell T2b A T2b tumor is based on its width. It is larger than 4 cm but no larger than 5 cm. For comparison, a golf ball is 4.3 cm. It may be invasive or affect the lung as described for a T2a tumor.
T3 A T3 tumor has one of these features: • Tumor is wider than than 5 cm but no larger than 7 cm • Invasive growth into the outer lining of the lung, heart lining, chest wall, azygos vein, a phrenic or chest spinal nerve, or stellate ganglion nerves • Multiple related tumors in the same lobe of the lung T4 A T4 tumor has one of these features: • Tumor is wider than than 7 cm • Invasive growth into the heart, a major blood vessel, windpipe, esophagus, diaphragm, thymus, spine, vagus nerve, or a spinal nerve in the throat • Related tumors in more than one lobe of the lung 35 NCCN Guidelines for Patients® Early & Locally Advanced Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer 5 Planning primary treatment N = Node score The N score describes cancer growth in nearby lymph nodes. Lymph nodes are small, bean-shaped structures located throughout your body that help fight disease. The N score is based on the spread of lung cancer to: h Lymph nodes in the lung h Lymph nodes just outside of the lung h Lymph nodes far from the lung The N scores used in this guide are N0, N1, N2a, N2b, and N3. Higher numbers mean greater spread of the cancer. A brief description of the N scores is in Guide 6.
M = Metastasis score The M score tells you if the cancer has spread to the lining around the lung or to other organs. The spread of cancer is called metastasis.
Lung cancer tends to travel to the brain, liver, adrenal glands, and bones and from one lung to the other.
M0 means the cancer has not spread far. M1 means the cancer has spread far. There are three M1 scores to describe where the cancer has spread: h M1a means the cancer has spread far within the chest. h M1b means the cancer has spread to one place beyond the chest. h M1c means the cancer has spread to more than one place beyond the chest.
Guide 6 N (node) scores used to stage lung cancer N0 The cancer has not spread to lymph nodes.
N1 The cancer has grown into or spread to lymph nodes in the lung.
N2a The cancer has spread to 1 lymph node in either of these places: • The middle of the chest next to the lung with cancer • Below the windpipe N2b The cancer has spread to 2 or more lymph nodes in one or both of these places: • The middle of the chest next to the lung with cancer • Below the windpipe N3 The cancer has spread to lymph nodes in one or more of these places: • The middle of the chest near the other lung • The other lung • Near the collarbone 36 NCCN Guidelines for Patients® Early & Locally Advanced Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer 5 Planning primary treatment Lung cancer stages There are 4 main stages of lung cancer. The cancer stages are further divided into subgroups and labeled with a letter. h Stage 1 consists of stages 1A and 1B h Stage 2 consists of stages 2A and 2B h Stage 3 consists of stages 3A, 3B, and 3C h Stage 4 consists of stages 4A and 4B The TNM scores are combined to assign a stage to the lung cancer. TNM scores with a better outlook have a lower cancer stage. Read which TNM scores correspond with a cancer stage in Guide 7.
All lung cancers are staged before treatment based on the tests described in prior chapters. The pretreatment stage is called the clinical stage.
If you have surgery, the cancer is staged again. The second stage is called the pathologic stage. It's based on tests of tissue removed from your body.
Treatment by clinical stage The clinical stage is very important for planning primary treatment. It helps predict the course of the cancer and which treatment is best. Options for primary treatment by clinical stage are noted in Guide 8.
When possible, surgery is the primary treatment of NSCLC. However, surgery isn’t an option if it’s unlikely that all the cancer can be removed.

Your team will make a final recommendation for treatment based on additional factors. These factors include any challenges to treatment, how well your lungs are working, and your overall health. Your team’s recommendation will also reflect your values and preferences.
Participating in a clinical trial A clinical trial may be an option for you.
A clinical trial is a type of medical research study. After being developed and tested in a lab, potential new ways of fighting cancer need to be studied in people.
If found to be safe and effective in a clinical trial, a drug, device, or treatment approach may be approved by the U.S. FDA.
Everyone with cancer should carefully consider all of the treatment options available for their cancer type, including standard treatments and clinical trials. Talk to your doctor about whether a clinical trial may make sense for you.
Phases Most cancer clinical trials focus on treatment and are done in phases. h Phase 1 trials study the safety and side effects of an investigational drug or treatment approach. h Phase 2 trials study how well the drug or approach works against a specific type of cancer. h Phase 3 trials test the drug or approach against a standard treatment. If the results are good, it may be approved by the FDA. h Phase 4 trials study the safety and benefit of an FDA-approved treatment.
Who can enroll?
It depends on the clinical trial’s rules, called eligibility criteria. The rules may be about age, cancer type and stage, treatment history, or I tell newly diagnosed lung patients that today there is HOPE and better treatments and outcomes to the disease. In the past decade, the survivor rate has been climbing every year." “ 39 NCCN Guidelines for Patients® Early & Locally Advanced Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer 5 Planning primary treatment general health. They ensure that participants are alike in specific ways and that the trial is as safe as possible for the participants.
Informed consent Clinical trials are managed by a research team. This group of experts will review the study with you in detail, including its purpose and the risks and benefits of joining. All of this information is also provided in an informed consent form. Read the form carefully and ask questions before signing it. Take time to discuss it with people you trust. Keep in mind that you can leave and seek treatment outside of the clinical trial at any time.
Will I get a placebo?
Placebos (inactive versions of real medicines) are almost never used alone in cancer clinical trials. It's common to receive either a placebo with a standard treatment, or a new drug with a standard treatment. You will be informed, verbally and in writing, if a placebo is part of a clinical trial before you enroll.
Are clinical trials free?
There is no fee to enroll in a clinical trial. The study sponsor pays for research-related costs, including the study drug. But you may need to pay for other services, like transportation or childcare, due to extra appointments. During the trial, you will continue to receive standard cancer care. This care is often covered by insurance.

Read this chapter to learn about the treatment you may have.
Planning treatment Surgery is used to treat most early-stage and many locally advanced non-small cell lung cancers (NSCLCs). Your team will decide if surgery is an option for you and if you need additional treatment.
Evaluation for surgery NCCN experts recommend finding a highly experienced, board-certified thoracic surgeon. Lung cancer surgery should be a major part of their practice.
Surgery may be an option for you if all of the cancer can be safely removed. To decide if you can safely undergo surgery, your surgeon will consider: h Where the cancer is inside and outside of your lungs h The health of your lungs h Your overall health Cancer that can be safely and completely removed is called resectable cancer.
Evaluation for additional treatment Resectable NSCLC is often treated with more than one type of treatment.
Treatment in addition to surgery may include: h A regimen of systemic therapy, which is one or more cancer drugs taken at a specific dose, schedule, and length of time (see Guide 9) h Radiation therapy to treat cancer that may remain near the surgical site h Sequential chemoradiation, treatment with chemotherapy then radiation therapy h Concurrent chemoradiation, receiving both treatments during the same time frame Additional treatment is based on several factors, including: h The type and stage of NSCLC h Your medical history, including medicines you take h Biomarker tests, including those for PD-L1 level, EGFR mutations, and ALK gene fusions Medical history and biomarkers tests are described in Chapter 3: Testing for early and locally advanced NSCLC.
43 NCCN Guidelines for Patients® Early & Locally Advanced Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer 6 Treating lung cancer with surgery Treatment before surgery Preoperative therapy is treatment received before surgery. It's sometimes called neoadjuvant therapy or induction therapy.
Preoperative therapy isn’t needed for stage 1A cancers because surgery alone has very good results. The 2 reasons that higher cancer stages have preoperative therapy as well as treatment options are explained next.
Reason 1: Preoperative instead of postoperative therapy For years, systemic therapy was started after surgery for many cancers. More recently, it’s become the first treatment because of less serious side effects.
Immune checkpoint inhibitors with chemotherapy NCCN experts recommend that care teams strongly consider giving immune checkpoint inhibitors with chemotherapy. This treatment may be an option when the lung tumor is at least 4 centimeters (cm) wide or the cancer has spread to lymph nodes.
Guide 9 Types of systemic therapy used before or after surgery for NSCLC Platinum-doublet chemotherapy Kills fast-growing cells including cancer cells • Chemotherapy drugs that contain platinum include carboplatin and cisplatin.
• Platinum-doublet chemotherapy combines a platinum drug with docetaxel (Beizray, Docivyx,Taxotere), etoposide (Etopophos), gemcitabine (Avgemsi), paclitaxel, pemetrexed (Axtle, Alimta, Pemfexy, Pemrydi RTU), or vinorelbine.
• Chemotherapy is given by a slow drip into a vein, called an infusion, and occurs in cycles of treatment days followed by days of rest.
Immune checkpoint inhibitor Restores the ability of immune T cells to kill cancer cells • Atezolizumab (Tecentriq), pembrolizumab (Keytruda), durvalumab (Imfinzi), and nivolumab (Opdivo) are given by infusion in cycles.
• Atezolizumab with hyaluronidase-tqjs (Tecentriq hybreza), pembrolizumab with berahyaluronidase alfa-pmph (Keytruda qlex), and nivolumab with hyaluronidase-nvhy (Opdivo qvantig) are injected under the skin.
Targeted therapy Stops chemical signals that tell lung cancer cells to grow • Alectinib (Alecensa) and osimertinib (Tagrisso) are pills that can be taken at home on treatment days of the cycle.

Reason 2: Making surgery easier Preoperative therapy may make surgery easier for some stage 2 and stage 3 cancers.
Superior sulcus tumors Superior sulcus tumors are a distinct subset of invasive lung cancers. They start at the top of the lung and typically grow into the chest wall.
Concurrent chemoradiation is the first treatment of superior sulcus tumors. The full course of chemotherapy may be completed after surgery. Learn more about this treatment in Chapter 8: Treating lung cancer with chemoradiation.
Invasive or large tumors Starting with either concurrent chemoradiation or systemic therapy is an option for: h Stage 2B and stage 3A cancers with T3 tumors that invaded the chest wall, windpipe, or the middle of the chest h Stage 3A cancers with T4 tumors that are invasive or larger than 7 centimeters Cancer in N2 nodes NSCLC with an N2 stage is sometimes treated with surgery. Systemic therapy or chemoradiation is given first to stop cancer growth before surgery.
Removing lung cancer Your surgeon will schedule surgery if there is a way to remove all the cancer. This section explains the different ways surgery is performed and the types of surgery used to remove the cancer.
Methods to perform surgery Your surgeon will remove tissue by one of two methods. The classic or open method is called thoracotomy. The newer method is a less invasive surgery called thoracoscopy. h Thoracotomy is performed through one large cut between the ribs. Surgical tools are inserted through the cut to remove the cancer. Sometimes, part of the rib needs to be removed, too. h Thoracoscopy is performed through several small cuts between the ribs. This surgery is sometimes called video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery because it's performed using a small video camera inserted through a cut.
Your surgeon may perform thoracoscopy using robotic arms to control the surgical tools. This approach is called robotic-assisted thoracoscopic surgery.
Types of lung surgery There are 5 types of lung surgery. To understand them, it’s important to know that the lungs have sections called lobes. The right lung has 3 lobes, and the left lung has 2 lobes. h Wedge resection removes a small part of a lobe. h Segmentectomy removes a large part of a lobe.
46 NCCN Guidelines for Patients® Early & Locally Advanced Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer 6 Treating lung cancer with surgery h Lobectomy removes an entire lobe and is preferred for most lung cancers. h Sleeve lobectomy removes an entire lobe and part of the main airway. h Pneumonectomy removes an entire lung.
Lung tumors that have grown through the lung wall into other tissue are removed in one piece. This surgery is called an en-bloc resection.
Your surgeon will remove the lung tumor with enough normal-looking tissue at its edge. This normal-looking tissue is called the surgical margin. The goal is to have no cancer cells in the margin so a cure is likely.
Types of lymph node surgery During surgery, your surgeon will also remove lymph nodes that have or may have cancer. To remove nodes, some organs may need to be moved or cut.
Lung cancer surgery There are 5 common lung cancer surgeries. The most common are lobectomy and pneumonectomy and are shown below. Sleeve lobectomy removes a lobe and part of the main airway called the bronchus. Wedge resection and segmentectomy remove only part of a lobe.
47 NCCN Guidelines for Patients® Early & Locally Advanced Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer 6 Treating lung cancer with surgery There are 2 types of lymph node surgery: h A systematic lymph node sampling removes some nodes in the lung and between the lungs. h A lymph node dissection removes as many nodes as possible from the lung and between the lungs.
Side effects of surgery Your care team will help you recover from surgery. They will provide care to prevent or relieve side effects.
Common side effects of any surgery are pain, swelling, and scars. Pain can be intense after lung surgery. Pain and swelling often fade away in the weeks after surgery.
Results of surgery After surgery, your surgeon and pathologist will rate the surgical margin around the removed tumor: h R0 means no cancer was found in the margin. h R1 means cancer was found in the margin with a microscope. h R2 means some of the visible cancer wasn’t removed.
The pathologist will also assess fluid samples and the removed lymph nodes for cancer. When lymph nodes farthest from the tumor don’t have cancer, it's likely that all nodes with cancer were removed.
Surgical margin The tumor will be removed, along with some normal-looking tissue around its rim. The normal-looking tissue is called the surgical margin. The surgical margin will be tested for cancer. Postoperative therapy is based on if there is cancer in the margins. 48 NCCN Guidelines for Patients® Early & Locally Advanced Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer 6 Treating lung cancer with surgery Treatment after surgery Postoperative therapy (also called adjuvant therapy) treats any cancer that wasn’t removed during surgery. It lowers the chance of cancer returning.
In this section, you’ll learn NCCN recommendations for which cancers need postoperative therapy and the types of postoperative therapy.
Treatment if there’s no cancer in surgical margins You may receive postoperative therapy even if margins are cancer-free, which is a rating of R0.
Some cancer may remain in your body because it wasn’t found with scans or seen during surgery and removed.
Systemic therapy is an option for stage 1B and stage 2A cancers but is needed for stage 2B and stage 3 cancers.
After systemic therapy, stage 3 cancers may be treated with radiation therapy.
Treatment if there’s cancer in surgical margins Postoperative therapy is needed when cancer is in the surgical margins. Surgical margins with cancer are rated either R1 or R2.
Second surgery A second surgery to remove all the cancer is an option for stage 1 and stage 2 cancers. After the second surgery, some stage 1B and stage 2A cancers and all stage 2B cancers are treated with systemic therapy.
Radiation therapy For stage 1 and stage 2A cancers, radiation therapy is an option when a second surgery is likely to cause serious health issues. Systemic therapy may be part of treatment for stage 1B and stage 2A cancers.
Chemoradiation For stage 2B cancers, chemoradiation is an option when a second surgery isn’t. For stage 3 cancers, chemoradiation is the only option for postoperative therapy. h Either sequential or concurrent chemoradiation is recommended for R1 margins. h Concurrent chemoradiation is recommended for R2 margins.
Options for systemic therapy Chemotherapy or targeted therapy is used for postoperative systemic therapy. If you had chemotherapy before surgery, you won't have it again. However, other types of systemic therapy may be restarted after surgery.
Platinum-doublet chemotherapy NCCN experts recommend postoperative platinum-doublet chemotherapy for: h Stage 1B and stage 2A cancers that are highly likely to return h Stage 2B and stage 3 cancers The regimen you’ll receive is based on the type of NSCLC and if treatment will include radiation. Regimens used with concurrent chemoradiation are listed in Chapter 8: Treating lung cancer with chemoradiation.

All treatments listed in this guide are recommended and appropriate. When helpful, NCCN experts also assign a level of preference to their recommendations for systemic therapies: h Preferred therapies have the most evidence they may work better and be safer than other therapies. h Other recommended therapies can provide effective results but may have less evidence, more side effects, or may not work quite as well as preferred therapies. h Therapies used in certain cases work best for individuals with specific cancer features or health circumstances. For NSCLC, carboplatin regimens are used when people can’t take cisplatin.
Targeted therapy Your team may recommend targeted therapy: h Osimertinib treats cancers with EGFR mutations. It’s an option if you can’t have chemotherapy. h Alectinib treats cancers with ALK gene fusions. It’s an option if the lung tumor was at least 4 centimeters wide or the cancer had spread to lymph nodes.

It may be used by itself to treat lung cancer or it can be combined with other treatments. This chapter explains when radiation therapy is used and how it works.
Uses of radiation therapy Radiation therapy uses high-energy x-rays or particles to treat lung cancer. The x-rays or particles damage cancer cells, which either die or stop making new cancer cells.
Radiation therapy is used in many ways to treat early and locally advanced non-small cell lung cancers (NSCLCs): h It's used as the main (also called primary) treatment of stage 1 and some stage 2 lung cancers. When the goal is to cure cancer, it's called definitive radiation therapy. h It's used with surgery as described in Chapter 6: Treating lung cancer with surgery. h It's combined with chemotherapy as described in Chapter 8: Treating lung cancer with chemoradiation.
A radiation oncologist is an expert in treating cancer with radiation. Your doctor will lead a team that designs your treatment plan and provides treatment.
Radiation therapy Radiation therapy is often delivered from a large machine. The x-rays or particles pass through skin and travel to the tumor. Modern treatments are able to protect healthy tissue.
54 NCCN Guidelines for Patients® Early & Locally Advanced Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer 7 Treating lung cancer with radiation therapy Types of radiation therapy External beam radiation therapy (EBRT) is the most common method used for lung cancer. A large machine makes radiation beams that are shaped to the form of the tumor. The machine aims the highest radiation dose at the tumor. A much lower dose is given to the nearby normal-looking tissue.
There are several common techniques of EBRT: h Intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT) delivers x-ray (photon) beams that very closely match the shape of the target and spares more normal tissue. h Stereotactic ablative radiotherapy (SABR) treats cancer with very precise, high-dose x-ray (photon) beams. It delivers a very high dose of radiation per treatment, so it's only given for a few treatments. Treatment is finished in 1 to 1½ weeks. h Proton therapy treats cancer with proton beams. Proton beams deliver radiation mostly within the tumor. h Three-dimensional conformal radiation therapy (3D-CRT) delivers an x-ray (photon) beam that matches the shape of the target but may not be as focused as IMRT. It's an older technique.
Radiation therapy is typically delivered daily Monday through Friday. Treatment visits are about 15 minutes for IMRT and 3D-CRT and 30 to 45 minutes for SABR and proton therapy. Some radiation oncologists deliver SABR treatment 2 to 3 times per week rather than every day.
Curing lung cancer with radiation Definitive EBRT is used when trying to cure stage 1 and stage 2 NSCLC. Any of the EBRT techniques described may be used, though NCCN experts prefer SABR for smaller tumors. SABR may be an option for some stage 2 cancers with large T3 tumors.
Overcoming treatment challenges A lung tumor is harder to target than some other tumors in the body. Lung tumors often move when you breathe. To account for these challenges, advanced methods may be used: h Four-dimensional computed tomography (4D-CT) may be used for treatment planning. It’s like a video, so your radiation oncologist will see how the tumor moves when you breathe. h Motion control methods may be used to keep the tumor still during treatment. h At times, your radiation oncologist may ask you to hold your breath for 15 to 20 seconds at a time to better target the tumor.
Adjuvant chemotherapy Adjuvant chemotherapy may be received after definitive radiation therapy. It treats cancer that radiation did not. For example, large tumors and very abnormal-looking cancer cells may have spread to places outside of the radiation field.
NCCN experts recommend that care teams consider chemotherapy for stage 2 cancers, especially for T2b and T3 tumors.
55 NCCN Guidelines for Patients® Early & Locally Advanced Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer 7 Treating lung cancer with radiation therapy The options for chemotherapy after surgery are also options for after radiation therapy. See Guide 12 and Guide 13 in Chapter 6.
Side effects of radiation Radiation therapy does not cause pain during a treatment session—you'll feel nothing at all. It also does not make you radioactive. But radiation therapy may cause health issues called side effects.
Facts about side effects Here are some important things to know: h Side effects differ by the type of radiation therapy. Most people have no side effects from SABR. Proton therapy may cause skin changes, but IMRT rarely does. h Side effects of radiation therapy are cumulative. This means they build up slowly and are worse at the end of treatment. h Adding chemotherapy to radiation therapy often causes more side effects. h Side effects that start during radiation therapy typically improve 2 to 4 weeks after treatment is finished.
Types of side effects During treatment, your radiation oncologist will see you about once a week to assess for possible side effects: h Fatigue is a common side effect of radiation therapy. h Skin changes in the treatment area may occur. Often, people describe skin changes as like a sunburn. For people with darker skin, radiation can cause the skin to darken and be painful. h Near the end of treatment, you may have pain when swallowing due to irritation to your esophagus. h Although not common, your lung may become inflamed after treatment, causing sudden shortness of breath or cough. These are symptoms of radiation pneumonitis. Call your radiation oncologist immediately if you have these symptoms.
Key points h Radiation therapy uses high-energy x-rays or particles to treat lung cancer. h Radiation therapy is used in several ways to treat lung cancer. When used to cure cancer, it's called definitive radiation therapy. h Radiation therapy is most often delivered from outside of the body using a large machine. h Several techniques are available to cure lung cancer, but stereotactic ablative radiotherapy (SABR) is preferred for smaller tumors. h You may receive systemic therapy to treat any cancer that radiation therapy did not. h Side effects from radiation build up over the course of treatment and typically improve 2 to 4 weeks after treatment is done.

It may be used to cure lung cancer. Read this chapter to learn about chemoradiation options.
Uses of chemoradiation Chemoradiation is a cancer treatment that combines chemotherapy and radiation therapy: h Chemotherapy uses drugs that stop the process by which cells make more cells, so it affects fast-growing cells like cancer cells. h Radiation therapy uses high-energy x-rays or particles to damage cancer cells. The cancer cells either die or can’t make more cancer cells.
Chemoradiation is sometimes received before or after surgery as described in Chapter 6: Treating lung cancer with surgery.
Chemoradiation may also be the main (also called primary) treatment of locally advanced lung cancer when surgery is not an option. When the goal is to cure cancer, it's called definitive chemoradiation.
About chemotherapy This section provides some important information about chemotherapy. Details about receiving radiation therapy are described in Chapter 7: Treating lung cancer with radiation therapy.
Doctors called medical oncologists prescribe chemotherapy. A chemotherapy regimen consists of one or more drugs that are taken at a specific dose, schedule, and length of time.
Chemotherapy Chemotherapy for lung cancer is a liquid that is injected into a vein. Some injections are done in the arm or hand while others are done though an implanted device called a port. An infusion is a slow drip controlled by a pump that may take hours.
59 NCCN Guidelines for Patients® Early & Locally Advanced Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer 8 Treating lung cancer with chemoradiation For non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), more than one type of chemotherapy is often received. Most commonly, cisplatin or carboplatin is used with another drug. This is called platinum-doublet chemotherapy.
You will not receive chemotherapy every day. Instead, it will be given in cycles of treatment days followed by days of rest. These cycles give your body a chance to recover after receiving chemotherapy.
You will need to go to a treatment center to get chemotherapy. The chemotherapy will be slowly injected into your vein. This is called an infusion. Chemotherapy travels in your bloodstream to treat cancer throughout your body.
Curing lung cancer with chemoradiation Definitive chemoradiation is a treatment option for some stage 2B and stage 3 cancers.
There are 2 scheduling approaches to deliver chemoradiation: h Concurrent chemoradiation means that chemotherapy and radiation therapy are given at the same time. h Sequential chemoradiation means you will first complete chemotherapy and then receive radiation therapy. This schedule may be followed if concurrent treatment is likely too harmful for you.
Chemotherapy options for chemoradiation Chemotherapy regimens used for chemoradiation are listed in Guide 14.
All treatments listed in this guide are recommended and appropriate. When helpful, NCCN experts also assign a level of preference to their recommendations for systemic therapies: h Preferred therapies have the most evidence they may work better and be safer than other therapies. h Other recommended therapies can provide effective results but may have less evidence, more side effects, or may not work quite as well as preferred therapies. h Therapies used in certain cases work best for individuals with specific cancer features or health circumstances. For NSCLC, carboplatin regimens are used when people can’t take cisplatin.
Schedule of radiation therapy Radiation therapy is typically delivered in 30 to 35 small doses, called fractions, over 6 to 7 weeks. For sequential chemoradiation, some people are treated with around 15 higher-dose fractions.
60 NCCN Guidelines for Patients® Early & Locally Advanced Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer 8 Treating lung cancer with chemoradiation Consolidation treatment Treatment given after chemoradiation is called consolidation treatment. The goals of consolidation are to bolster the results of treatment and improve the chance of a cure.
There are 2 options for consolidation treatment after definitive concurrent chemoradiation: h Osimertinib (Tagrisso) for lung cancers with an EGFR exon 19 deletion or L858R mutation h Durvalumab (Imfinzi) for lung cancers without an EGFR exon 19 deletion or L858R mutation Osimertinib is a cancer drug called an EGFR kinase inhibitor. EGFR is a cell protein that helps start cell growth. Osimertinib stops the activity of EGFR and, in turn, lowers the number of new cancer cells being made. It's a pill that can be taken at home.
Durvalumab is a cancer drug called an immune checkpoint inhibitor. It works by enabling immune T cells to attack cancer cells. It's given by infusion.
Guide 14 Regimens for chemoradiation to treat non-small cell lung cancer Sequential chemoradiation Concurrent chemoradiation Adenocarcinoma, large cell carcinoma, and rare cell types Preferred therapies: • Cisplatin, Pemetrexed Other recommended therapies: • Cisplatin, Vinorelbine • Cisplatin, Etoposide Therapies used in certain cases: • Carboplatin, Paclitaxel • Carboplatin, Pemetrexed Preferred therapies: • Carboplatin, Pemetrexed • Cisplatin, Pemetrexed • Carboplatin, Paclitaxel • Cisplatin, Etoposide Squamous cell carcinoma Sequential chemoradiation Preferred therapies: • Cisplatin, Gemcitabine • Cisplatin, Docetaxel Other recommended therapies: • Cisplatin, Vinorelbine • Cisplatin, Etoposide Therapies used in certain cases: • Carboplatin, Paclitaxel • Carboplatin, Gemcitabine Concurrent chemoradiation Preferred therapies: • Carboplatin, Paclitaxel • Cisplatin, Etoposide 61 NCCN Guidelines for Patients® Early & Locally Advanced Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer 8 Treating lung cancer with chemoradiation Treatment side effects Side effects are unwanted health issues caused by treatment. They differ between people based on the type and length of treatment as well as the person.
Side effects from chemotherapy are caused by the death of fast-growing normal cells. Examples include nausea and vomiting, anemia, and hair loss. Side effects are typically worse with concurrent chemoradiation than with sequential chemoradiation.
Immune checkpoint inhibitors can cause your immune cells to attack healthy cells in your body. Side effects include rash, mouth pain, and fatigue.
Management of side effects is discussed in Chapter 4: Improving life with supportive care.
Key points h Chemoradiation is a treatment with both chemotherapy and radiation therapy. It may be used to try to cure lung cancer. h Chemotherapy for lung cancer often consists of a drug made with platinum and one other drug. It's slowly infused into a vein. h For chemoradiation, chemotherapy and radiation therapy are typically given at the same time, but sometimes chemotherapy is given first. h More treatment may be received after chemoradiation to improve the chance of a cure. This is called consolidation.
Questions to ask h How did you decide what type of chemoradiation is best for me? h What is the schedule, or cycles, of the chemotherapy? h Do I need consolidation treatment? h What are the common and serious side effects of my treatments? h How will you prevent side effects and relieve the side effects I have?
What’s next? Once there are no signs of cancer, surveillance is started. Surveillance is ongoing testing for the return of cancer. It is a part of survivorship care. Survivorship care also focuses on the management of long-term and late effects of cancer. To learn more, read Chapter 9: Lifelong survivorship care.
62 NCCN Guidelines for Patients® Early & Locally Advanced Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer 9 Lifelong survivorship care 63 Coordinated health care 63 Ongoing testing to find cancer early 65 Managing physical and mental effects 65 Addressing social and financial needs 65 Preventing disease 66 Key points 66 Questions to ask 63 NCCN Guidelines for Patients® Early & Locally Advanced Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer 9 Lifelong survivorship care Survivorship care often begins after initial cancer treatment ends. Its focus is on the wide and lasting impact of cancer and its treatment. Survivorship care will help you recover from cancer and prevent disease.
Coordinated health care When survivorship care starts, it's very important that your health care providers work together to give you ongoing, coordinated care. At this stage, you’ll see your primary care provider more often and see non-cancer specialists as well.
As part of survivorship care, NCCN recommends: h Routine blood pressure, cholesterol, and glucose monitoring h Routine dental exams h Bone density testing if needed h Pulmonary rehabilitation if needed You will also have follow-up visits with your cancer care team. They will test for cancer and assess for side effects as explained next.
Ongoing testing to find cancer early While non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) can sometimes be cured, it's very important to watch for the return of the cancer. The return of cancer is called a recurrence. It's also important to be checked for other types of cancer.
Surveillance for recurrence Survivorship care includes a schedule of health visits and tests to check for recurrence. Pulmonary rehabilitation As part of survivorship care, you may see more health specialists. People who have chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) or pulmonary hypertension commonly receive pulmonary rehabilitation. If you had lung surgery, your team may refer you to pulmonary rehabilitation.
64 NCCN Guidelines for Patients® Early & Locally Advanced Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer 9 Lifelong survivorship care These ongoing checkups for recurrence are called surveillance. Surveillance is started when there are no signs of cancer after treatment.
If your care team detects a recurrence early, it will allow for timely treatment. At follow-up visits, you will need to update your medical history, get physical exams, and undergo CT (computed tomography) scans. Some people may have a MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) scan of their brain. A schedule of surveillance tests is listed in Guide 15.
Screening for second cancers You are at risk for a second cancer. Anyone who has been treated and cured of one lung cancer is at risk for a new lung cancer. Also, a second cancer is a possible late effect of some cancer treatments.
More information on second cancers is in NCCN Guidelines for Patients: Survivorship Guide 15 Surveillance after treatment of non-small cell lung cancer Stage 1 or stage 2 cancers that were not treated with radiation therapy Every 6 months for 2 to 3 years, see your care team for a: • Medical history • Physical exam • CT scan of the chest with or without contrast If results are normal, then repeat every year: • Medical history • Physical exam • Low-dose CT scan of the chest Stage 1 or stage 2 cancers that were treated with radiation therapy and All stage 3 cancers Every 3 to 6 months for 3 years, see your care team for a: • Medical history • Physical exam • CT of the chest with or without contrast If results are normal, then repeat every 6 months for 2 years: • Medical history • Physical exam • CT scan of the chest with or without contrast If results remain normal, then repeat every year: • Medical history • Physical exam • Low-dose CT scan of the chest 65 NCCN Guidelines for Patients® Early & Locally Advanced Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer 9 Lifelong survivorship care Care for Cancer-Related Late and Long-Term Effects, available at NCCN.org/ patientguidelines and on the NCCN Patient Guides for Cancer app.
Cancer screening involves routine testing for cancer before its symptoms start. You may enroll in a screening program if you have an average risk for prostate, breast, cervical, colorectal, and skin cancers.
Managing physical and mental effects Cancer and its treatment can cause unwanted health issues. These issues are called complications, adverse events, or side effects.
Many side effects of treatment quickly resolve after treatment ends. But during survivorship care, your team will continue to assess for side effects.
Long-term effects start during treatment and persist after treatment is done. Less often, late effects from the cancer or treatment start long after treatment has ended.
NCCN Guidelines for Patients: Survivorship Care for Cancer-Related Late and Long-Term Effects discuss management of many effects, including: h Heart disease h Lymphedema h Chemobrain h Fatigue and sleep-wake disorders h Pain h Distress and mental health Addressing social and financial needs You may have social and financial needs during or after lung cancer treatment. As part of survivorship care, your team will continue to ask you about food, housing, health insurance, and other needs.
A common issue during survivorship is deciding on whether to return to work. Your health care providers can help you. Information on returning to work is in NCCN Guidelines for Patients: Survivorship Care for Cancer-Related Late and Long-Term Effects.
Preventing disease Another part of survivorship care is preventing diseases. This section conveys recommendations from NCCN lung cancer experts.
Vaccinations Many vaccines safely prevent infections in people with a history of lung cancer. You may get the following vaccines as needed: h Flu shot every year h COVID-19 vaccine h Shingles vaccine h Pneumococcal vaccine with revaccination h Hepatitis vaccine 66 NCCN Guidelines for Patients® Early & Locally Advanced Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer 9 Lifelong survivorship care Healthy living It’s important for everyone to start or keep a healthy lifestyle—but it’s even more important for people who’ve had cancer. Healthy living may improve your health and well-being. It may also help prevent cancer from returning.
Common goals for healthy living include: h No smoking h Being physically active and avoiding inactivity h Eating healthful foods and drinking little or no alcohol h Managing body weight to maintain or improve health h Routine sun protection More information on preventing poor health can be found in NCCN Guidelines for Patients: Survivorship Care for Healthy Living.
Key points h It’s important that your health care providers work together to address all of your needs. h You'll have regular tests to check for a return of lung cancer and for new cancers. h Your team will assess ongoing side effects as well as new ones at follow-up visits. They will also ask if you have social and financial challenges. h Healthy living and vaccines may improve your health and prevent disease.
Questions to ask h How will you coordinate care with my other health care providers? h How can late side effects be prevented or treated? h Who can I talk to about help with paying bills, returning to work, and other needs? h Which vaccines do I need? h What goals for healthy living do you recommend for me?
What’s next? It’s common to have many concerns about cancer. Your care team will help you. More sources of support are listed in Chapter 10: Other resources.

bedrock_calls.system_prompt:
You are an HTA and Market Access strategist extracting structured evidence from one source document for a JCA (Joint Clinical Assessment) comparator and outcome scoping request.

You will be told the REQUESTED INTERVENTION and the REQUESTED POPULATION. Extract every distinct claim the document makes that is relevant to comparator or outcome scoping.

CRITICAL - DO NOT HALLUCINATE:
- Use ONLY information explicitly stated in the provided text. Never use outside medical knowledge to fill a gap, infer a typical dose, assume a standard comparator, or complete a partial fact with what is usually true.
- If a field is not explicitly stated, its value MUST be an empty string. Never invent a value to avoid leaving something blank.
- Do not paraphrase in a way that adds specificity the text did not have.

FIELD DEFINITIONS - read these; they are not self-evident:

subject_drug: the drug this specific claim is ABOUT - the treatment being assessed, studied or recommended in the passage you are extracting from. A document about a disease often discusses several drugs. If the passage is about a DIFFERENT drug than the requested intervention, say so here. Never write the requested intervention's name unless the passage is genuinely about it.

comparator.as_stated: the treatment this claim names as a comparison, alternative or standard of care - exactly as the source words it, including a regimen's full component list. A drug name, a named regimen, or a legitimate generic category the source states as the most specific thing available ("best supportive care", "physician's choice of chemotherapy"). NOT a sentence, NOT a trial name, NOT a statistical annotation.

comparator.role - choose exactly one:
  "active_comparator"  - studied, recommended or required AS the comparison for the subject drug in the population this passage describes
  "prior_therapy"      - treatment the patient RECEIVED BEFORE reaching this population (e.g. an induction regimen preceding a maintenance-phase question). This is treatment history, NOT a comparator
  "background_therapy" - given to all arms as a backbone, not the thing being compared
  "intervention_arm"   - this IS the subject drug's own arm, not a comparator
  "unclear"            - the passage does not let you tell
Getting this wrong is the single most common error: an induction-phase backbone named near the right population is prior therapy, not a comparator.

comparator.components: for a combination regimen, the complete list of substances AS ONE SOURCE STATES THEM. Never pool components from two different regimens that share an ingredient.

comparator.comparator_scenario - from the source's own language, choose one:
  "unique" (names one comparator) | "each_required" (several, required together) |
  "at_least_one" (several, at least one acceptable) | "individualised" (a bundle of options chosen by patient characteristics)

comparator.retain_all_status: "confirmed_droppable" or "confirmed_must_retain" ONLY when the source itself states a droppability preference. Otherwise "unconfirmed" - which will be the case for the great majority of sources, because this is a procedural preference, not a clinical fact. Never infer it.

DO NOT populate any drug class or mechanism for the comparator. That is resolved downstream from the comparator's own substance identity. If you write a class here it will be the SUBJECT drug's class, which is the exact error this instruction prevents.

population_context.*: the disease/population context THE SOURCE ITSELF states for this claim, in the source's own words - distinct from the requested population, which may be broader or narrower. Fill line_of_therapy, prior_therapy, stage, biomarker and treatment_setting_intent with what THIS passage says, never with the requested population's own label. If the passage states an interval since prior therapy or since relapse, put it in "other".

recommendation_strength (clinical guidelines only): "preferred" | "conditional_alternative" | "not_recommended" | "not_stated", as the guideline itself grades it. Never present a conditional or alternative recommendation as preferred.

outcome.measure: the outcome or endpoint named.
outcome.result: the reported figure, if any, exactly as stated.
outcome.unit: the unit of measurement EXACTLY as the source reports it (e.g. "months, median", "% of patients", "HR (95% CI)") - never invented, never assumed from general knowledge of what a typical unit would be.
outcome.instrument: the named instrument, where the source names one (e.g. a specific questionnaire). Empty otherwise.
outcome.is_requirement: true when the source states this outcome as one an assessment REQUIRES or EXPECTS in scope (an HTA methods document, an assessment scope table, a guideline's stated outcome set). false when the source is merely REPORTING a result for it. These are different things and the distinction matters more than the value.
outcome.requirement_type: "relative_effect_required" | "descriptive_only" | "" - only when the source states it.

evidence_quote: a VERBATIM span copied from the text that contains this claim. It must appear character-for-character in the text. If you cannot copy such a span, omit the whole record rather than paraphrasing.
evidence_locator: where in the document it sits (section heading, table number, page), if the text makes that visible.

member_state: the country whose body/guideline this claim belongs to, when the document is a national source. "EU-wide" for an EU-level record. Empty if unclear.

MULTIPLE POPULATIONS IN ONE DOCUMENT: a document can describe several populations for the same drug. Output SEPARATE records, one per population the text actually describes. Each comparator stays attached to the population it was ACTUALLY reported against - never pulled into the requested population's record just because the same document also discusses that population elsewhere.

Return ONLY a JSON array, no preamble, no markdown fences. Empty array if the document contains nothing relevant:

You are an HTA and Market Access strategist extracting structured evidence from one source document for a JCA (Joint Clinical Assessment) comparator and outcome scoping request.

You will be told the REQUESTED INTERVENTION and the REQUESTED POPULATION. Extract every distinct claim the document makes that is relevant to comparator or outcome scoping.

CRITICAL - DO NOT HALLUCINATE:
- Use ONLY information explicitly stated in the provided text. Never use outside medical knowledge to fill a gap, infer a typical dose, assume a standard comparator, or complete a partial fact with what is usually true.
- If a field is not explicitly stated, its value MUST be an empty string. Never invent a value to avoid leaving something blank.
- Do not paraphrase in a way that adds specificity the text did not have.

FIELD DEFINITIONS - read these; they are not self-evident:

subject_drug: the drug this specific claim is ABOUT - the treatment being assessed, studied or recommended in the passage you are extracting from. A document about a disease often discusses several drugs. If the passage is about a DIFFERENT drug than the requested intervention, say so here. Never write the requested intervention's name unless the passage is genuinely about it.

comparator.as_stated: the treatment this claim names as a comparison, alternative or standard of care - exactly as the source words it, including a regimen's full component list. A drug name, a named regimen, or a legitimate generic category the source states as the most specific thing available ("best supportive care", "physician's choice of chemotherapy"). NOT a sentence, NOT a trial name, NOT a statistical annotation.

comparator.role - choose exactly one:
  "active_comparator"  - studied, recommended or required AS the comparison for the subject drug in the population this passage describes
  "prior_therapy"      - treatment the patient RECEIVED BEFORE reaching this population (e.g. an induction regimen preceding a maintenance-phase question). This is treatment history, NOT a comparator
  "background_therapy" - given to all arms as a backbone, not the thing being compared
  "intervention_arm"   - this IS the subject drug's own arm, not a comparator
  "unclear"            - the passage does not let you tell
Getting this wrong is the single most common error: an induction-phase backbone named near the right population is prior therapy, not a comparator.

comparator.components: for a combination regimen, the complete list of substances AS ONE SOURCE STATES THEM. Never pool components from two different regimens that share an ingredient.

comparator.comparator_scenario - from the source's own language, choose one:
  "unique" (names one comparator) | "each_required" (several, required together) |
  "at_least_one" (several, at least one acceptable) | "individualised" (a bundle of options chosen by patient characteristics)

comparator.retain_all_status: "confirmed_droppable" or "confirmed_must_retain" ONLY when the source itself states a droppability preference. Otherwise "unconfirmed" - which will be the case for the great majority of sources, because this is a procedural preference, not a clinical fact. Never infer it.

DO NOT populate any drug class or mechanism for the comparator. That is resolved downstream from the comparator's own substance identity. If you write a class here it will be the SUBJECT drug's class, which is the exact error this instruction prevents.

population_context.*: the disease/population context THE SOURCE ITSELF states for this claim, in the source's own words - distinct from the requested population, which may be broader or narrower. Fill line_of_therapy, prior_therapy, stage, biomarker and treatment_setting_intent with what THIS passage says, never with the requested population's own label. recommendation_strength (clinical guidelines only): "preferred" | "conditional_alternative" | "not_recommended" | "not_stated", as the guideline itself grades it. Never present a conditional or alternative recommendation as preferred.

outcome.measure: the outcome or endpoint named.
outcome.result: the reported figure, if any, exactly as stated.
outcome.unit: the unit of measurement EXACTLY as the source reports it (e.g. "months, median", "% of patients", "HR (95% CI)") - never invented, never assumed from general knowledge of what a typical unit would be.

Namn Form Styrka Förp. Varunr. AIP (SEK) AUP (SEK) Stivarga Filmdragerad tablett 40 mg 84 190054 26109,00 26677,43 UTREDNING I ÄRENDET Stivarga (regorafenib) är en multikinashämmare som har en bred aktivitet och inhiberar flera olika proteinkinaser. Stivarga är indicerat för behandling av vuxna patienter med o metastaserande kolorektal cancer (CRC) som tidigare har behandlats med, eller inte anses vara lämpade för tillgängliga behandlingar. Till dessa hör fluoropyrimidinbaserad kemoterapi, en anti-VEGF-behandling och en anti-EGFR-behandling.
o icke resektabla eller metastaserande gastrointestinala stromacellstumörer (GIST) som har progredierat under eller varit intoleranta mot tidigare behandling med imatinib eller sunitinib.
Företaget har tidigare ansökt om att Stivarga ska ingå i läkemedelsförmånerna för indikationen metastaserande kolorektal cancer (dnr. 3527/2013, avslag) samt för indikationen icke resektabla eller metastaserande GIST (dnr. 2624/2015, bifall med begränsning till GIST-indikationen). Stivarga är avsett för oral användning. Den rekommenderade dosen av Stivarga är 160 mg (4 tabletter om 40 mg) en gång dagligen i 3 veckor följt av 1 vecka utan behandling. Denna 4-veckorsperiod utgör en behandlingscykel. Behandlingen ska fortsätta så länge patienten bedöms ha nytta av läkemedlet eller tills oacceptabel toxicitet uppstår. Kolorektal cancer är den tredje vanligaste cancerformen hos män och kvinnor i Sverige. Ungefär 6000 personer per år diagnostiseras med kolorektal cancer. 20-25 procent har metastaserande sjukdom vid diagnos och ungefär lika många får metastaser senare i förloppet. Överlevnaden är starkt beroende av tumörstadiet vid diagnos. Vid metastaserande kolorektal cancer är behandlingen oftast palliativ och syftar till att minska eller förebygga uppkomst av tumörrelaterade symptom, förlänga tid till progression samt att öka totalöverlevnaden. Behandling med principiellt tre olika typer av cytostatika samt antikroppar mot VEGF och EGFR används i dagsläget i olika kombinationer. Många patienter får två eller tre linjers behandling där kombinationen byts ut vid svikt på tidigare behandling. Socialstyrelsens riktlinjer från 20141 anger evidensen för regorafenib vad gäller effekt som måttlig och läkemedlet har lägsta prioritering, 10 (skala 1-10). Avgörande för 1 Socialstyrelsen, ”Nationella riktlinjer för tjock- och ändtarmscancer”, 2014 3 (8) 776/2016 rekommendationen är att tillståndet har mycket stor svårighetsgrad och att åtgärden ger liten effekt till en hög till mycket hög kostnad per kvalitetsjusterat levnadsår. Dessutom anges det att åtgärden innebär risk för biverkningar. I det nationella vårdprogrammet för kolorektal cancer2 står det att: ”Effekten är mycket begränsad (medianöverlevnaden förlängdes med 1,4 mån, tumörremission hos 1 % av patienterna i den pivotala studien) och regorafenib har för närvarande (mars 2015) inte någon plats i rutinsjukvården.” I ett annat dokument, som uppdateras årligen, där användningen av målinriktade behandlingar värderas och rekommenderas av Gastrointestinal Onkologisk Förening (GOF), omnämns regorafenib som singelbehandling i terapisituationen ”palliativ medicinsk behandling efter progress på 5-FU, Irino och Oxalibaserad CT samt Beva och EFGR-antikropp med rekommendationen att avstå” år 20153. Kommentar till detta lyder: ”Majoriteten av patienterna hade haft metastatisk sjukdom minst 18 mån före studiestart. En tydlig relativ behandlingsvinst observerades men absolutvinsten var liten och bedöms inte stå i proportion till biverkningarna.” I årets (2016) GOF4-dokument har evidensen för nytta graderats till måttlig, vilket betyder att tillräckligt vetenskapligt stöd finns för att åtgärden ska vara tillämpbar i rutinsjukvården men där nytta-/riskförhållandet eller den sammanlagda evidensnivån inte är sådan att åtgärden alltid ska vara en del av rutinsjukvården. Man konstaterar också att absolutvinsten är liten och bör ställas i relation till relativt uttalade biverkningar. Stivarga har i en stor randomiserad placebokontrollerad studie (CORRECT, fas III) visat på statistiskt signifikant bättre effekt jämfört mot placebo vad gäller total överlevnad (se fig. 1), progressionsfri överlevnad samt sjukdomskontroll efter 6 veckors behandling. Fig. 1. Total överlevnad för patienterna som fick regorafenib (röd, övre) eller placebo (blå, nedre) i CORRECT-studien efter 2:a planerade cut-off5. Företaget har genomfört en mindre dubbelblind fas III studie, CONCUR. Design och upplägg av denna studie är mycket likt det för CORRECT-studien. AIP (SEK) AUP (SEK) Lonsurf, tablett Tablett 15mg/6,14mg 20 57979 5435,00 5589,95 Lonsurf, tablett Tablett 15mg/6,14mg 60 158698 16305,00 16677,35 Lonsurf, tablett Tablett 20mg/8,19mg 20 516182 7246,67 7437,85 Lonsurf, tablett Tablett 20mg/8,19mg 60 389330 21740,00 22221,05 2 (6) 1088/2016 ANSÖKAN Servier Sverige AB har ansökt om att läkemedlet Lonsurf, tablett, ska ingå i läkemedelsförmånerna och att pris fastställs, i enlighet med tabell på sida 1. UTREDNING I ÄRENDET Lonsurf innehåller de aktiva substanserna trifluridin och tipiracilhydroklorid. Trifluridin är en tymidinbaserad nukleosidanalog och tipiracilhydroklorid är en tymidinfosforylas-hämmare. Lonsurf är avsett för behandling av vuxna patienter med metastaserande kolorektalcancer som tidigare har behandlats med, eller inte anses vara lämpliga kandidater för, tillgängliga behandlingar inklusive fluoropyrimidin-, oxaliplatin- och irinotekanbaserad kemoterapi, anti-VEGF-medel och anti-EGFR-medel. Den rekommenderade startdosen av Lonsurf till vuxna är 35 mg/m2/dos (max 80 mg/dos) administrerat oralt två gånger dagligen på dag 1–5 och 8–12 av varje 28-dagarscykel, så länge nytta kan observeras eller tills oacceptabel toxicitet uppstår. Kolorektal cancer är den tredje vanligaste cancerformen hos män och kvinnor i Sverige. Ungefär 6000 personer per år diagnostiseras med kolorektal cancer. 20-25 procent har metastaserande sjukdom vid diagnos och ungefär lika många får metastaser senare i förloppet. Överlevnaden är starkt beroende av tumörstadiet vid diagnos. Behandling av metastaserande kolorektal cancer är oftast palliativ och syftar till att minska eller förebygga uppkomst av tumörrelaterade symptom, förlänga tid till progression samt att öka totalöverlevnaden. Principiellt tre olika typer av cytostatika samt antikroppar mot VEGF och EGFR används i dagsläget i olika kombinationer. Många patienter får två eller tre linjers behandling där kombinationen byts ut vid svikt på tidigare behandling. Ett nytillkommet alternativ är tyrosinkinashämmaren Stivarga (regorafenib) som i praktiken har indikation mot samma patientgrupp som kommer att behandlas med Lonsurf. Lonsurf omnämns inte i Socialstyrelsens riktlinjer, nationella vårdprogrammet eller i riktlinjerna från Gastrointestinal Onkologisk Förening (GOF). Läkemedlet omnämns dock i de senaste riktlinjerna från European Society for Medical Oncology (ESMO) som ett nytillkommet alternativ för behandling av metastaserande kolorektal cancer i sista behandlingslinjen där också Stivarga ingår.
